18	# RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
19	
20	- Authors: Bai, Shuai; Deng, Jiayong; Fan, Sicheng; Fu, Yikun; Gao, Chang; Hu, Xuhao
21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.22000 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22000
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Version read: arXiv v2, 21 Sep 2026 (p. 1). **Preprint, not peer-reviewed.** Industry paper (Alibaba Group, p. 1).
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Build environments to both evaluate and train "hybrid" computer-use agents (CUAs): agents that combine GUI operation (looking at and clicking an interface) with coding and command-line work, and decide themselves when to explore, implement and verify (p. 1-2).
30	- [A] The vehicle is **application recreation**: given only a running reference application, the agent must discover its behaviour and build a faithful, runnable reimplementation with no prescribed workflow; the running reference acts as an oracle for hidden behavioural tests (p. 1, p. 3).
31	- [A] Secondary aims: show that recreation trajectories are useful training data that transfer to other coding and computer-use benchmarks (p. 3, p. 5-6), and analyse how agents work and what their rebuilt applications look like (p. 11).
32	
33	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
34	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions [I], based on the section structure (p. 5-18): (a) how well do frontier agents recreate applications across five platforms; (b) does training on verified recreation trajectories transfer out of distribution; (c) how do agents explore, implement and verify; (d) how do recreated artifacts differ structurally from their references; (e) which behaviours fail most.
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark and environment paper with (i) a held-out benchmark evaluation of ten frontier models, (ii) a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) transfer experiment with two model initialisations, (iii) a paired auxiliary comparison of two tool interfaces, and (iv) descriptive trajectory, artifact and failure analyses plus case studies (p. 5-6, p. 10-20, p. 38-47).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Agent gets a task prompt, interactive access to the running reference, and an environment with GUI control and development tools; it returns source that must build and launch (desktop source + build/launch scripts; Android Gradle project -> APK; Web scaffolded source -> self-contained `index.html` on a pinned React stack); only observable behaviour is scored, not architecture (p. 3, p. 7). Desktop and Android are source-blind; on Web the served client code is necessarily visible (p. 7). Each rollout has a 20-hour wall-clock budget (p. 4, p. 28).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Ten models with their scaffolds: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol via Codex; Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Qwen3.8-Max-0902 and Qwen3.7-Plus via Claude Code, with listed context windows, output caps and reasoning settings (p. 28). For transfer: each run's first evaluated checkpoint (p. 1, p. 6). [I] No human-developer baseline is reported (checked p. 10-11, p. 28).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] Native references from open-source GitHub repositories (desktop) and GitHub/F-Droid projects (Android), pinned to upstream commits; Web from 44 benchmark-authored synthetic sites and 6 openly licensed real sites (e.g. postgresql.org, webpack.js.org) (p. 7-8, p. 27). Training tasks from open-source GUI apps on GitHub, deduplicated against the evaluation sets (p. 5).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 250 tasks (applications/websites), 50 per platform (p. 7). Median production source of references: Ubuntu 49.3k, macOS 13.5k, Windows 6.7k, Android 15.0k LOC (p. 8). 81 tasks package 393 fixture files (p. 8, p. 34). Training: 35,000 trajectories (7,000 per platform) (p. 5). One example app has 85 rule-based tests and 35 visual assertions (p. 20). [I] Total number of test cases across the suite: not reported (checked p. 8-9, p. 32-34).
44	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Excluded libraries, frameworks, extensions and apps needing login or remote services; references must run reproducibly; survivors balanced on domain, framework, source size, feature complexity and upstream activity (p. 8, p. 31-32). Android apps with first-run dialogs were patched to remove them (p. 31). Web pages screened by an agent on eight criteria, then human review (p. 32).
45	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Benchmark, environments and test suites released via a website, GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope (p. 1, p. 27); per-task licence metadata provided (p. 26-27). The PDF shows link labels, not URLs; release not checked by us.
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Task-isolated, versioned VM/container workers per rollout (p. 4); platform actions exposed as direct MCP tool calls (qwen-cua-driver 0.7.3 on desktop, mobile-mcp 0.1.5, Playwright MCP 0.0.79) (p. 5, p. 28). Isolation: unprivileged agent user, protected reference and test files, default-deny network egress on Ubuntu/macOS/Windows/Web; Android lacks an attested packet-level egress filter and the installed APK is recoverable in principle (p. 9-10, p. 36-38). Test generation: an orchestrator agent combines source or page analysis with runtime exploration, subagents write tests per category ("lanes": structure, menu, button, computation, state, text on desktop) (p. 8, p. 32-33); every case replayed on a clean reference, unstable ones discarded, then human review before freezing (p. 8-9). Transfer: SFT of Qwen3.7-Plus and an in-house Qwen-Flash-CPT checkpoint on trajectories generated by Qwen3.8-Max and filtered by rejection sampling on the verifiers (p. 5-6); each OOD benchmark run once per task per checkpoint with a Claude Code scaffold (p. 6, p. 28-29).
49	- Not reported [I] (checked p. 5-11, p. 28-29): number of human test reviewers and their agreement; rollouts per task per model in the main benchmark; SFT hyper-parameters.
50	- [I] The main benchmark is probably a single rollout per task. The one-rollout direct-MCP arm of the Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 comparison (Prog 35.05, VLM 31.00; p. 11) reproduces the Table 11 Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 scores exactly (35.05 / 31.00; p. 30). This is not stated explicitly.
51	- Code availability: [A] Harness, runners, evaluation code and configurations released on GitHub (p. 27); not checked.
52	
53	## 6. Evaluation metrics
54	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
55	  - [V] **Programmatic score (Prog)**: fraction of frozen, reference-validated test cases passed, reading exact text, widget state, navigation, persistence or computed values through the platform accessibility/automation API (AT-SPI, AXUIElement, UI Automation, UiAutomator, DOM/ARIA); Web weights checks by specificity (p. 9). A candidate that fails to build or launch scores zero; unreached cases fail (p. 9).
56	  - [V] **VLM score**: binary verdicts from a Qwen3.7-Plus judge (temperature 0) on reference-grounded natural-language assertions about candidate screenshots, for rendered properties the accessibility tree does not expose (p. 9, p. 32).
57	  - [V] **Average score** = mean of Prog and VLM; apps macro-averaged within platform, platforms weighted equally (p. 9, p. 11). **Prog >= 90% / = 100%** = share of apps (near-)fully passing (p. 11).
58	  - [V] Chosen because they are implementation-agnostic: tests depend on observable behaviour, not source similarity, so agents may choose any architecture (p. 4, p. 8).
59	  - [V] Artifact metrics: production LOC (cloc), file count, largest-file share, UI framework family (p. 15-16, p. 30-31). Process metrics: interaction breadth, windows inspected, controlled input variation, final-loop closure, tool-call composition, hacking attempts, tokens and cost (p. 12-15).
60	  - [V] Suite coverage audit: 77% of cases leave the start surface, 24% traverse 2+ surfaces, 94.2% check an interaction outcome, 40.7% require an exact value (p. 9).
61	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Trajectory and resource figures show 95% bootstrap intervals (p. 12, p. 14); size-association slopes have cluster-bootstrap 95% intervals, which include zero on Ubuntu and Android (p. 31). [I] Main benchmark scores are point estimates with no confidence intervals in Table 3 or Table 11 (p. 11, p. 30); no significance tests between models and no judge-vs-human agreement are reported (checked p. 9, p. 11, p. 28-32).
62	
63	## 7. Key findings
64	1. Recreation is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra leads with 58.19 Prog / 57.92 VLM / 58.06 average, then Claude Opus 5 (44.16) and GPT-5.6 Sol (42.06); Grok 4.6 is fourth (36.73) and Qwen3.7-Plus is lowest (9.15) — [V] (p. 1, p. 11). (Table 3 column headers are scrambled in the text layer; the mapping was checked against Figure 1's ranked model list (p. 1) and word positions in the PDF (p. 11).)
65	2. Full functional fidelity is rare: GPT-6 Astra reaches Prog >= 90% on 17.6% and Prog = 100% on 2.8% of apps; every other model reaches at most 5.53% and 0.8% — [V] (p. 11, p. 16).
66	3. Agents reproduce what an interface contains better than what it does (four analysed models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max-0902; p. 12, p. 17): structure has the highest pass rate in 15 of 16 native model-platform comparisons; the weakest category (button, computation or interaction) trails structure by 9.1-34.4 points; on Web, static content beats interaction by 28.2-36.7 points — [V] (p. 16-17). Example: a recreation with 100.0% VLM but only 55.1% Prog (p. 18).
67	4. Rebuilt apps are much smaller and more concentrated: 89.4% have less production source than the reference (median LOC ratio 16.9%); 92.3% use fewer files; 83.8% put a larger share of code in the largest file; median files 4-43 (recreations) vs 47-167 (references); largest-file share 10-64% vs 5-21% — [V] (p. 15-16). Recreation size barely tracks reference size (log-log slopes 0.08-0.23) — [V] (p. 15). Scope: four models analysed (Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max-0902); desktop and Android only for reference comparisons; coverage varies across model-platform cells (p. 12, p. 15). [I] Per-cell denominators are not reported (checked p. 15-16, p. 30-31).
68	5. More code does not mean higher fidelity: Claude Opus 5 has the highest median recreation LOC on all five platforms **among the four analysed models**, while GPT-6 Astra has the lowest on four of five — [V] (p. 15); robust to a common-project restriction (p. 31). Scope as in finding 4 (p. 12, p. 15).
69	6. Agents often switch frameworks (same four models; Web excluded): 75% of Ubuntu/macOS deliverables whose references use Electron, Tauri or Wails switch to native GTK or AppKit/SwiftUI; on Windows 50% of non-.NET references are rebuilt in WPF or WinForms — [V] (p. 16). [A] Authors read this as "architectural substitution rather than implementation quality" (p. 16).
70	7. Verification habits are weak: the strict final edit -> relaunch -> inspect sequence appears in only 23.6-47.5% of trajectories; controlled input variation in 13.4-17.0% — [V] (p. 12, p. 17-18). Scope: four models analysed (Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max-0902) (p. 12). [I] Trajectory counts per model-platform cell are not reported (checked p. 12-15).
71	8. Contamination check: exact-line overlap between recreations and references (four models) has medians of 0.014-0.088% and maxima below 3.2% — [V] (p. 18). Agents do attempt shortcuts (network egress, protected paths, package extraction), most often GLM-5.3 among the four analysed models — [V] (p. 13). Two Web case studies replayed reference content. Ablira (72.73% Prog / 40.79% VLM, p. 46) was caught by the scrape detector, so the 0.10 aggregate cap applies (p. 38, p. 47); [I] the case table therefore shows its pre-penalty channel scores (based on the min(s, 0.10) rule, p. 9, p. 38). Kartova escaped detection and kept 54.82% Prog / 14.63% VLM (34.72% average) — [V] (p. 47).
72	9. Transfer: both SFT runs finish above their first measured checkpoint on all five out-of-distribution benchmarks (gains up to 17.9 points), but curves are not monotonic — [V] (p. 3, p. 6). [A] Authors call this "initial evidence" and "exploratory" because budgets and harness revisions differ (p. 3, p. 29).
73	10. A programmable SDK interface (one rollout, 50 Windows apps, Claude Opus 4.8) kept quality similar (Prog 35.05 vs 35.60) while cutting estimated cost from $90.50 to $41.58 and wall-clock time from 4.12 to 3.04 h per task — [V] (p. 11).
74	
75	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
76	- [A] Pinned, reproducible environments limit coverage of live services, changing external state and real users (p. 21).
77	- [A] Hidden suites sample a finite set of outcomes, so passing them "cannot establish equivalence across all states and interaction paths" (p. 22).
78	- [A] Public references may be in pretraining data; source-overlap screening cannot rule out memorisation or all source reuse (p. 22, p. 18).
79	- [A] Trajectory and artifact comparisons are descriptive; model identity, harness and runtime vary together, so no behaviour is shown to cause higher scores (p. 3, p. 11, p. 16).
80	- [A] Android isolation is weaker (no attested egress filter; installed APK recoverable) and Web cannot be source-blind (p. 7, p. 10, p. 37).
81	- [A] OOD transfer runs differ in budgets and harness revisions and are "exploratory evidence" (p. 29). Android commit identifiers were mostly inferred and are not verified pinned revisions (p. 30).
82	- [A] Scores are not comparable with the earlier in-house version reported in a blog post (p. 27).
83	
84	## 9. Limitations we identified
85	- [I] **Conflict of interest not declared.** All authors are from Alibaba (p. 1); the training data are generated by Qwen3.8-Max, the VLM judge is Qwen3.7-Plus, the desktop driver is Qwen Code's, and Qwen models are among those evaluated (p. 5, p. 9, p. 28). No COI statement. Qwen3.7-Plus, which is also the VLM judge (p. 9), is the lowest-scoring evaluated model (VLM 9.12, average 9.15, p. 11). So no favourable self-scoring is visible, but judge self-preference was not tested.
86	- [I] **No variance.** Rollouts per task are not reported for the main benchmark and no CIs are given for Table 3 (p. 11); with 20-hour stochastic agent runs, small model differences may not be stable. The main benchmark is probably a single rollout per task: the one-rollout direct-MCP arm (p. 11) reproduces the Table 11 Windows / Claude Opus 4.8 scores exactly (p. 30). This is not stated explicitly.
87	- [I] **Judge and reviewer reliability unknown.** The VLM judge's accuracy against humans and the number/agreement of human test reviewers are not reported (p. 8-9).
88	- [I] **Scaffold confound.** GPT models run in Codex, all others in Claude Code (p. 28), so model and harness are entangled in the main ranking.
89	- [I] **Unexplained denominators.** Claude Opus 5's Web Prog >= 90% of 13.64% (p. 30) cannot come from 50 tasks (every value would be a multiple of 2.00, as the other cells in that row are); it fits 6/44 (or 3/22). The paper invalidates runs that fail isolation checks (p. 9) and reports evaluator-valid subsets elsewhere (p. 11, p. 20), so some runs were probably excluded. The number of excluded runs per model and platform is not reported.
90	- [I] **Score integrity gap.** A transformed replay (Kartova) evaded the scrape detector and kept 54.82% Prog / 14.63% VLM (p. 47). The detected replay (Ablira, p. 47) falls under the 0.10 aggregate cap (p. 38), so its reported 72.73% / 40.79% (p. 46) are pre-penalty channel scores. How often undetected replay occurs across the Web suite is not reported.
91	- [I] **Transfer design is uncontrolled.** Improvements are measured from the first evaluated checkpoint (p. 6); whether that checkpoint is the untrained initialisation is not stated. Each OOD benchmark is run once per task (p. 28), the curves are non-monotonic (p. 6), and there is no control SFT mixture (e.g. equally long non-recreation agent trajectories; none described, p. 5-6, p. 29). Recreation-specific transfer is therefore not separated from generic agentic SFT or run-to-run noise. "Gains of up to 17.9 percentage points" (p. 3) is a single best-case last-vs-first difference with no uncertainty.
92	- [I] **Code quality only as size/structure.** LOC, file count, largest-file share and framework (p. 15-16) are crude proxies; no complexity, duplication, smells, tests or maintainability measures. "More monolithic" is suggestive for our RQ3 but not a maintainability assessment.
93	- [I] **Web scores are panel-relative.** The Web discriminativeness gate re-runs the suite on "rebuilds from a panel of models" and removes assertions every model passes (p. 34), making Web scores depend on that panel. The panel's composition is not reported; if it overlaps with the evaluated models, Web scores are partly defined by the evaluated models themselves.
94	
95	## 10. Threats to validity
96	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Strong isolation design (p. 9-10, p. 36-38) and an overlap audit (p. 18) reduce leakage, but Android and Web are weaker by design (p. 7, p. 10), and hacking attempts occur (p. 13). Model and scaffold are confounded (p. 28). Patched Android references (p. 31) differ from upstream builds.
97	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Open-source, offline, login-free apps of moderate size (p. 8); Web is mostly synthetic (44 of 50, p. 7). Results may not hold for commercial apps with backends, accounts or network services.
98	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Prog and VLM measure agreement with a finite, reference-validated test sample (p. 22), with depth and specificity audited (p. 9) — a good proxy for functional and visual fidelity but not equivalence. Size and file metrics are not code-quality measures (p. 16).
99	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] 50 apps per platform; no CIs on main scores; bootstrap CIs on secondary analyses (p. 12, p. 14, p. 31); slopes not distinguishable from zero on two platforms (p. 31).
100	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] High: pinned environments, versions, model configs, licence metadata and release of benchmark and harness (p. 26-28). Proprietary model endpoints and unreported SFT hyper-parameters limit replication of the transfer experiment.
101	
102	## 11. Future research directions
103	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 22): controlled online and multi-user workflows; broader hidden-test coverage across states and interaction paths; newly constructed references to reduce contamination risk. Improvement targets for agents: collect targeted evidence about state transitions and validate the exact submitted artifact (p. 18).
104	- Suggested by us [I]: (a) add maintainability measures (complexity, duplication, modularity, test presence) to the artifact analysis and relate them to Prog/VLM; (b) run several rollouts per task and report CIs; (c) validate the VLM judge against human ratings; (d) include a human-developer recreation baseline.
105	
106	## 12. Relevance to our research
107	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3 (partial), RQ4, RQ5.
108	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest match so far to "AI-assisted reverse engineering": agents rebuild whole apps from a running reference across five platforms (RQ1). It gives the strongest benchmark evidence on functional fidelity (RQ2): high average scores hide that full behavioural equivalence is rare and that interactions and computations fail more than static UI. It provides the only structural comparison of rebuilt vs original code we have seen in this set (RQ3: smaller, fewer files, more concentrated, frequent framework substitution), though not real maintainability metrics, and only for four of the ten models and for desktop and Android references (p. 12, p. 15). Its evaluation design (reference-validated hidden tests in two channels, coverage audit, isolation, contamination audit) and its gaps (no variance, judge validity, COI) are directly useful for RQ4 and for designing our own study. The missing link between fidelity and maintainability is a concrete RQ5 gap. [I] Directionally consistent with [@chen2025iwr]. Static structure outperforms action-conditioned behaviour within bai's programmatic tests (p. 16-17), but bai's visual channel does not exceed its programmatic channel in aggregate: VLM is below Prog for 9 of 10 models, the exception being GPT-5.6 Sol at 43.49 vs 40.63 (p. 11). The two papers measure the gap differently.

18	# IWR-Bench: Can LVLMs reconstruct interactive webpage from a user interaction video?
19	
20	- Authors: Chen, Yang; Liu, Minghao; Shen, Yufan; Li, Yunwen; Huang, Tianyuan; Fang, Xinyu
21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2509.24709 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24709
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Version read: arXiv v3, 19 Nov 2025 (p. 1). **Preprint, not peer-reviewed.**
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Introduce and formalise Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR): given a video of a user interacting with a webpage plus the page's static assets, a model must generate code that reproduces both the visual appearance and the interactive behaviour seen in the video (p. 4, p. 5).
30	- [A] Motivation: existing webpage-to-code benchmarks are static (screenshot-to-code, e.g. Design2Code, WebSight) or treat interactions as single-step, stateless events (Interaction2Code), and do not provide the static assets needed for a realistic rebuild (p. 2, p. 6).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] Central question: "Can LVLMs reconstruct the dynamic, interactive functionalities of a webpage from observing a user interaction video?" (p. 2).
34	- [I] No formal hypotheses are stated; the study is a descriptive benchmark evaluation (p. 7-9).
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a cross-sectional comparison of 28 large vision-language models (LVLMs) on the same tasks, scored automatically by an "agent-as-a-judge" that replays a ground-truth action sequence on the generated page (p. 4, p. 6-8).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each model receives the interaction video (sampled at 1 fps, max 64 frames) and a composite image of all crawled static assets, and must output one self-contained `index.html` with all HTML, CSS and JS; backend logic must be mocked in JS; no external libraries or fonts (p. 8, p. 20). Asset filenames are anonymised (e.g. `asset_001.png`) so models must match assets visually rather than by name (p. 5).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [I] No method baseline is described (checked pp. 7-9). [V] The comparison is across 28 models in three groups: 17 proprietary MLLMs, 9 open-source MLLMs, 2 open-source video-specialised models; three models are also run in "thinking" (reasoning-enhanced) and non-thinking variants (p. 8). [I] Because those three thinking variants are counted separately, the 28 entries cover 25 distinct base models (based on Table 3, p. 8).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] Live real-world websites; 113 tasks from 100 websites; videos recorded by trained annotators while a browser extension logs action type and parameters; static assets collected with automated crawlers plus manual inspection (p. 1, p. 5).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 113 tasks/videos; 1,001 actions in total (mean 8.9 per video); 620 actions carry a visual checkpoint and 403 carry a logical assertion; mean video length 35.4 s (max 172.9 s); 19 unique resolutions; 10.62% mobile (p. 6). Interaction-logic mix: L1 static 7.96%, L2 simple state 47.79%, L3 complex workflow 33.63%, L4 algorithm/game 10.62% (p. 3).
44	- Sampling / selection method: [V] 200 candidate tasks proposed by web-development experts -> deduplication and diversity balancing across domain, visual complexity and interaction logic -> 161 -> cross-verification by a second annotator and an LLM check of assertions -> disputed, ambiguous or overly trivial tasks removed -> 113 (p. 5-6). [I] Exact criteria for "trivial" or "disputed" are not reported.
45	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Benchmark and evaluation code "will be made publicly available" at https://github.com/SIGMME/IWR-Bench (p. 1). We did not check whether the release happened.
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Video sampled at 1 fps, capped at 64 frames (longer videos uniformly downsampled); video frames and asset image given as a sequential multi-image input; "All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended by the model providers" (p. 8). A standard system prompt is used for all models (p. 18, p. 20). Evaluation executor built on the `browser-use` library; Gemini-2.5-Pro is the MLLM judge for logical assertions and for the high-level visual score (p. 6-7). Actions target elements by natural-language description rather than coordinates (p. 17). [I] Number of runs per model, temperature/seed and variance: not reported (checked pp. 7-9, 17).
49	- Evaluator determinism: [A] The executor is described as "deterministic" (p. 6). Which model resolves the natural-language element descriptions (p. 17) into page elements, and whether replays are repeatable, is not reported.
50	- Code availability: [A] Announced for release at the GitHub link above (p. 1); not verified by us.
51	
52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
54	  - [V] **IFS (Interactive Functionality Score)** = successful actions / total actions; an action succeeds only if it is operationally feasible (target element found) and all its logical assertions pass (p. 7). Chosen to measure functional correctness, because pixel-wise metrics "cannot appraise functionality" (p. 3).
55	  - [V] **VFS (Visual Fidelity Score)** = macro-average over reached checkpoints with a visual flag of 0.5 x low-level score (mean of OCR Levenshtein text similarity and DINO cosine similarity) + 0.5 x high-level MLLM score (p. 7). The MLLM rubric weights Layout 10, Elements 15, Content and Text 40, Style 15, Overall 20 points (p. 20).
56	  - [V] **Final Score** = 0.7 x IFS + 0.3 x VFS, macro-averaged across the benchmark (p. 7).
57	  - [V] Weights w = 0.5 and alpha = 0.7 were chosen by grid search to maximise Spearman's rho with human judgements of 60 instances (20 random tasks x 3 random models) rated by five PhD-level students; best rho = 0.57 for VFS and 0.65 for the Final Score (p. 17). [I] Agreement among the five raters is not reported; their judgements were aggregated (p. 17).
58	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [I] None found for model comparisons: Table 3 and the results text give single point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests (checked pp. 8-9, 16-19). [V] Only Spearman correlations are reported, for metric calibration (p. 17).
59	
60	## 7. Key findings
61	1. Interactive reconstruction from video is far from solved: GPT-5 is best with Final 36.35, IFS 24.39, VFS 64.25; no model exceeds 25 IFS — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
62	2. IFS is below VFS for every model: e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 VFS 61.34 vs IFS 22.29; GPT-4o (latest) VFS 57.55 vs IFS 17.55 — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [I] Caveat: the two scores do not share a denominator. VFS is computed only over checkpoints that were successfully reached (p. 7), IFS over every action in the trajectory (p. 7), so part of the gap is built into the metric definitions (see §9). The low absolute IFS (finding 1) does not depend on this caveat.
63	3. Hierarchy: the top eight models by Final Score are all proprietary (GPT-5 36.35 down to GPT-4.1 31.99); proprietary models span Final 16.50-36.35; the best open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking), scores 31.15 and is above 9 of the 17 proprietary models; video-specialised models are lowest (VideoLLaMA3-7B 13.67, InternVideo-2.5-Chat-8B 10.07) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). So the proprietary and open-source ranges overlap. [A] Authors conclude general multimodal reasoning and code generation matter more than video-specialised architectures (p. 9).
64	4. Thinking variants raise IFS and Final slightly in all three pairs: Claude-Sonnet-4 Final 34.62 vs 34.00 (IFS 23.65 vs 22.29); Claude-Opus-4 34.13 vs 33.33 (IFS 23.61 vs 21.83); Gemini-2.5-Pro 30.36 vs 30.31 (IFS 21.65 vs 20.51). But they lower VFS in all three pairs: 60.20 vs 61.34; 58.67 vs 60.18; 50.67 vs 53.18 — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [A] The authors describe the gains as "Consistent but Moderate" (p. 9); this goes beyond the data, given the VFS drops and the Gemini Final difference of 0.05 points.
65	5. Final Score drops sharply from static L1 tasks to interactive ones: GPT-5 61.85 on L1 vs 35.43 / 35.12 / 25.26 on L2 / L3 / L4 — [V] (p. 17). L1 is the highest category for every model, but L2 and L3 are similar and their order varies by model (e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 31.04 vs 32.86; Claude-Opus-4 (thinking) 31.52 vs 32.57; GPT-4.1 30.32 vs 31.98) — [V] (p. 17). By visual category, Final Score is lowest on data-dense layouts (GPT-5 26.05 on V4 vs 44.77 on V1), with V3 above V2 (43.77 vs 30.73) — [V] (p. 18). By domain, Life & Community is the weakest and Entertainment & Media the strongest (GPT-5 22.80 vs 47.24) — [V] (p. 19). All three category tables report Final Score only, not IFS or VFS (p. 16). So they do not show whether functional or visual fidelity drives the differences. [I] The robust contrast is L1 vs the rest; strata are small (about 9 L1 and 12 L4 tasks, see §9).
66	6. Judge reliability: three PhD students watched the agent run on 100 random generated pages; agent evaluation failed in only three cases (ambiguous element descriptors), which were then fixed — [V] (p. 9).
67	7. Case studies show distinct failure points, e.g. a model completing filter and sort but failing "add to cart"; a model failing to merge tiles in a 2048 rebuild; missing first-step elements blocking all later actions — [V] (p. 19-21).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- Not reported: the paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section (checked pp. 1-21). Design notes and disclosures that are not limitations (alternative weighting rejected, p. 7; agent-evaluation errors fixed, p. 9; LLM-assisted editing, p. 21) are recorded in Analyst notes.
71	
72	## 9. Limitations we identified
73	- [I] **IFS and VFS are not comparable in scale.** VFS averages only over checkpoints that were "successfully reached" (p. 7). It therefore cannot be lowered by functional failures that block later states. IFS divides successful actions by all actions in the trajectory (p. 7). Part of the IFS < VFS gap is therefore a property of the metrics, not only of the models. The authors mention unreachable states only to justify alpha = 0.7 (p. 7). How VFS is scored for a task where no visual checkpoint is reached is not reported. This weakens the headline "visual is solved better than function" reading. It does not weaken the finding that IFS is low in absolute terms.
74	- [I] **No code-quality or maintainability measurement.** The task forces a single self-contained HTML file with no libraries (p. 20), and only behaviour and appearance are scored. The benchmark therefore says nothing about code structure, readability or maintainability (our RQ3), and the single-file format is far from how real apps are built.
75	- [I] **Judge overlap.** Gemini-2.5-Pro is both the assertion/visual judge (p. 7) and one of the evaluated models (p. 8). Self-preference bias is not tested; its mid-table rank makes a large bias unlikely, but it is not ruled out.
76	- [I] **Moderate human alignment, tuned in-sample.** The weights were chosen to maximise rho on the same 60 instances used to report rho = 0.57 / 0.65 (p. 17); there is no held-out check. These are moderate correlations, so the Final Score is only partly aligned with human judgement. Agreement among the five raters is not reported (p. 17). The same is true of agreement among the three PhD students who observed the agent (p. 9).
77	- [I] **Evaluator re-scoring after fixes unclear.** The 3/100 agent failures were "rectified" (p. 9). Whether all 28 x 113 evaluations were re-run after the fixes is not reported. Element resolution from natural-language descriptions (p. 17) may itself involve a model, so the "deterministic" label (p. 6) is an author claim we cannot check.
78	- [I] **No variance reporting.** Single point estimates with default sampling settings (p. 8) and no repeated runs reported; several model gaps are tiny (e.g. 30.36 vs 30.31, p. 9) and could be noise.
79	- [I] **Unclear failure propagation.** It is not stated whether a failed early action stops the replay or whether later actions are still attempted (p. 7); Case 4 suggests failures cascade (p. 21). This affects how IFS should be read.
80	- [I] **Possible contamination.** Tasks come from popular live websites (e.g. an IMDb mock in Figure 2, p. 2); models may have seen similar code in training. Asset anonymisation (p. 5) reduces name cues but not memorised page structure. Not discussed by the authors.
81	- [I] **Small strata.** L1 (about 9 tasks) and L4 (about 12 tasks), derived by us from the percentages on p. 3, give unstable per-category scores.
82	
83	## 10. Threats to validity
84	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Task filtering removed "overly trivial" and "disputed" tasks without stated criteria (p. 6), which may shift difficulty. All models get identical inputs and prompt (p. 18), which supports a fair comparison. Video downsampling to at most 64 frames (p. 8) may remove interaction evidence from long videos (max 172.9 s, p. 6); this affects all models equally but penalises long tasks.
85	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Front-end only, one HTML file, mocked backend (p. 20); 113 tasks. Results do not transfer directly to multi-file apps, backends, or native desktop/mobile apps.
86	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] IFS measures replay of one ground-truth trajectory, not general behavioural equivalence; VFS mixes OCR, DINO and an MLLM rubric in which text content carries 40 of 100 points (p. 20). Both are proxies for "functional fidelity" and "visual fidelity". They also use different denominators: VFS covers only reached checkpoints, IFS all actions (p. 7). So the size of the IFS-VFS gap is partly metric-induced and should not be read as a direct comparison of the two capabilities. The fixed alpha = 0.7 encodes a value judgement (functionality matters more), supported only by rho = 0.65 (p. 17).
87	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs, tests or repeated runs (p. 8-9); conclusions about small differences (thinking vs non-thinking) are not statistically supported.
88	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts are published in the appendix (p. 20-21) and data and code are promised (p. 1). Proprietary model versions, default sampling settings and a proprietary judge model (p. 7) limit exact reproduction.
89	
90	## 11. Future research directions
91	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9): focus on "temporal reasoning, dynamic asset binding, and robust code synthesis"; structured code generation and state management as key directions (p. 9).
92	- Suggested by us [I]: (a) add code-quality/maintainability measures (static analysis, modularity) to IWR-style tasks so fidelity and code quality are measured together (our RQ5); (b) allow multi-file or framework-based outputs and agentic, iterative generation; (c) report repeated runs with variance and a held-out human-alignment set; (d) use a judge model that is not also evaluated.
93	
94	## 12. Relevance to our research
95	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirectly). Not RQ3.
96	- How it informs our work [I]: IWR-Bench is a direct example of AI "reverse engineering" an application from observable behaviour (a video) rather than from a written spec, so it fits RQ1. Its main result is central evidence for RQ2: functional correctness is low for every model (IFS < 25), and IFS sits far below VFS. The size of that gap is partly a product of how VFS is defined (only reached checkpoints, see §9). Its metric design (action replay with an agent judge, visual composite, human-calibrated weights) and weaknesses (no variance, in-sample calibration, judge overlap) inform RQ4 and our own study design. It illustrates the gap behind RQ5: fidelity is measured, but code quality and maintainability are not. [I] The result is directionally consistent with [@bai2026recreationworld], which finds static structure reproduced better than action-conditioned behaviour within its programmatic tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16-17]. However, bai's visual channel is not higher than its programmatic channel in aggregate [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11]. The two papers measure the gap differently, and here the gap is partly metric-induced (see §9). The convergence supports "static structure is easier than interaction logic". It does not support "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity".
97

18	# ProgramDistill: From Interactive Web Apps to Verifiable Reference-Guided SWE Tasks
19	
20	- Authors: Kim, Jeonghye; Kim, Minseon; Kim, Young Jin; Pereira, Matheus; Côté, Marc-Alexandre; Sordoni, Alessandro; Yuan, Xingdi; Shi, Zhengyan
21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed; v1 dated 16 Sep 2026). Affiliations: KAIST, Microsoft Research Montréal, Microsoft AI (p. 1).
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.18805 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18805
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	- PDF version analysed: arXiv v1, "arXiv:2609.18805v1 [cs.SE] 16 Sep 2026" (p. 1), from arxiv.org/pdf/2609.18805. No peer-reviewed version is known.
25	
26	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

29	## 1. Research objective
30	- [A] Evaluate coding agents on "reference-guided" software engineering: inferring intended behaviour by interacting with a working web application, then implementing it in an incomplete or empty application. This differs from benchmarks where behaviour is given as an issue or instruction (p. 1).
31	- [A] Turn working interactive web apps into a scalable, automatically built source of verifiable tasks ("application-to-task factorization") with controllable difficulty ("restoration depth") (p. 2).
32	
33	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
34	- Not stated as formal RQs. [A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). [I] Implicit empirical questions: how well agents restore masked features and rebuild whole apps from a live reference, how performance changes with the number of dependent behaviours, and why agents fail.
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
38	- Approach / model / intervention:
39	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
40	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
42	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
43	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
45	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
46	
47	## 4. Dataset and sample
48	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
49	- Sample size (N) and unit:
50	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
52	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
53	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
54	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
55	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
56	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
57	
58	## 5. Experimental setup
59	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
60	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
61	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
62	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
63	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
64	- [V] Number of runs, full reconstruction: 36 runs = 12 apps x 3 models (p. 11; p. 12). [I] Partial reconstruction: the number of runs per task is not stated. No variance is reported, so presumably one run each. Repeats or seeds: not reported.
65	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
66	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
67	
68	## 6. Evaluation metrics
69	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
70	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
71	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
72	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
73	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
74	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
75	
76	## 7. Key findings
77	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
78	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
79	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
80	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
81	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
82	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
83	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
84	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
85	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
86	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).
87	
88	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
89	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
90	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
91	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
92	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
93	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
94	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
95	
96	## 9. Limitations we identified
97	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry, with application state kept in `context.state` "so the verifier can reset it" (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
98	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
99	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
100	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
101	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
102	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
103	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
104	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
105	- [I] The abstract places the full-reconstruction results under "Across nine frontier coding agents" (p. 1; same wording p. 2), but only 3 models were evaluated in that setting (p. 11). Synthesis should not describe 49.2% as best-of-nine.
106	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: apparently one run per cell (runs per task not stated for partial reconstruction), full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
107	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
108	
109	## 10. Threats to validity
110	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
111	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
112	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
113	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
114	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
115	
116	## 11. Future research directions
117	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
118	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
119	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
120	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
121	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
122	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
123	- Suggested by us [I]:
124	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
125	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
126	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
127	  4. Add repeated runs.
128	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
129	
130	## 12. Relevance to our research
131	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
132	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.
133

18	# IWR-Bench: Can LVLMs reconstruct interactive webpage from a user interaction video?
19	
20	- Authors: Chen, Yang; Liu, Minghao; Shen, Yufan; Li, Yunwen; Huang, Tianyuan; Fang, Xinyu
21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2509.24709 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24709
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Version read: arXiv v3, 19 Nov 2025 (p. 1). **Preprint, not peer-reviewed.**
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Introduce and formalise Interactive Webpage Reconstruction (IWR): given a video of a user interacting with a webpage plus the page's static assets, a model must generate code that reproduces both the visual appearance and the interactive behaviour seen in the video (p. 4, p. 5).
30	- [A] Motivation: existing webpage-to-code benchmarks are static (screenshot-to-code, e.g. Design2Code, WebSight) or treat interactions as single-step, stateless events (Interaction2Code), and do not provide the static assets needed for a realistic rebuild (p. 2, p. 6).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [A] Central question: "Can LVLMs reconstruct the dynamic, interactive functionalities of a webpage from observing a user interaction video?" (p. 2).
34	- [I] No formal hypotheses are stated; the study is a descriptive benchmark evaluation (p. 7-9).
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a cross-sectional comparison of 28 large vision-language models (LVLMs) on the same tasks, scored automatically by an "agent-as-a-judge" that replays a ground-truth action sequence on the generated page (p. 4, p. 6-8).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each model receives the interaction video (sampled at 1 fps, max 64 frames) and a composite image of all crawled static assets, and must output one self-contained `index.html` with all HTML, CSS and JS; backend logic must be mocked in JS; no external libraries or fonts (p. 8, p. 20). Asset filenames are anonymised (e.g. `asset_001.png`) so models must match assets visually rather than by name (p. 5).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [I] No method baseline is described (checked pp. 7-9). [V] The comparison is across 28 models in three groups: 17 proprietary MLLMs, 9 open-source MLLMs, 2 open-source video-specialised models; three models are also run in "thinking" (reasoning-enhanced) and non-thinking variants (p. 8). [I] Because those three thinking variants are counted separately, the 28 entries cover 25 distinct base models (based on Table 3, p. 8).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] Live real-world websites; 113 tasks from 100 websites; videos recorded by trained annotators while a browser extension logs action type and parameters; static assets collected with automated crawlers plus manual inspection (p. 1, p. 5).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 113 tasks/videos; 1,001 actions in total (mean 8.9 per video); 620 actions carry a visual checkpoint and 403 carry a logical assertion; mean video length 35.4 s (max 172.9 s); 19 unique resolutions; 10.62% mobile (p. 6). Interaction-logic mix: L1 static 7.96%, L2 simple state 47.79%, L3 complex workflow 33.63%, L4 algorithm/game 10.62% (p. 3).
44	- Sampling / selection method: [V] 200 candidate tasks proposed by web-development experts -> deduplication and diversity balancing across domain, visual complexity and interaction logic -> 161 -> cross-verification by a second annotator and an LLM check of assertions -> disputed, ambiguous or overly trivial tasks removed -> 113 (p. 5-6). [I] Exact criteria for "trivial" or "disputed" are not reported.
45	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Benchmark and evaluation code "will be made publicly available" at https://github.com/SIGMME/IWR-Bench (p. 1). We did not check whether the release happened.
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Video sampled at 1 fps, capped at 64 frames (longer videos uniformly downsampled); video frames and asset image given as a sequential multi-image input; "All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended by the model providers" (p. 8). A standard system prompt is used for all models (p. 18, p. 20). Evaluation executor built on the `browser-use` library; Gemini-2.5-Pro is the MLLM judge for logical assertions and for the high-level visual score (p. 6-7). Actions target elements by natural-language description rather than coordinates (p. 17). [I] Number of runs per model, temperature/seed and variance: not reported (checked pp. 7-9, 17).
49	- Evaluator determinism: [A] The executor is described as "deterministic" (p. 6). Which model resolves the natural-language element descriptions (p. 17) into page elements, and whether replays are repeatable, is not reported.
50	- Code availability: [A] Announced for release at the GitHub link above (p. 1); not verified by us.
51	
52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
54	  - [V] **IFS (Interactive Functionality Score)** = successful actions / total actions; an action succeeds only if it is operationally feasible (target element found) and all its logical assertions pass (p. 7). Chosen to measure functional correctness, because pixel-wise metrics "cannot appraise functionality" (p. 3).
55	  - [V] **VFS (Visual Fidelity Score)** = macro-average over reached checkpoints with a visual flag of 0.5 x low-level score (mean of OCR Levenshtein text similarity and DINO cosine similarity) + 0.5 x high-level MLLM score (p. 7). The MLLM rubric weights Layout 10, Elements 15, Content and Text 40, Style 15, Overall 20 points (p. 20).
56	  - [V] **Final Score** = 0.7 x IFS + 0.3 x VFS, macro-averaged across the benchmark (p. 7).
57	  - [V] Weights w = 0.5 and alpha = 0.7 were chosen by grid search to maximise Spearman's rho with human judgements of 60 instances (20 random tasks x 3 random models) rated by five PhD-level students; best rho = 0.57 for VFS and 0.65 for the Final Score (p. 17). [I] Agreement among the five raters is not reported; their judgements were aggregated (p. 17).
58	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [I] None found for model comparisons: Table 3 and the results text give single point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests (checked pp. 8-9, 16-19). [V] Only Spearman correlations are reported, for metric calibration (p. 17).
59	
60	## 7. Key findings
61	1. Interactive reconstruction from video is far from solved: GPT-5 is best with Final 36.35, IFS 24.39, VFS 64.25; no model exceeds 25 IFS — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
62	2. IFS is below VFS for every model: e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 VFS 61.34 vs IFS 22.29; GPT-4o (latest) VFS 57.55 vs IFS 17.55 — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [I] Caveat: the two scores do not share a denominator. VFS is computed only over checkpoints that were successfully reached (p. 7), IFS over every action in the trajectory (p. 7), so part of the gap is built into the metric definitions (see §9). The low absolute IFS (finding 1) does not depend on this caveat.
63	3. Hierarchy: the top eight models by Final Score are all proprietary (GPT-5 36.35 down to GPT-4.1 31.99); proprietary models span Final 16.50-36.35; the best open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking), scores 31.15 and is above 9 of the 17 proprietary models; video-specialised models are lowest (VideoLLaMA3-7B 13.67, InternVideo-2.5-Chat-8B 10.07) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). So the proprietary and open-source ranges overlap. [A] Authors conclude general multimodal reasoning and code generation matter more than video-specialised architectures (p. 9).
64	4. Thinking variants raise IFS and Final slightly in all three pairs: Claude-Sonnet-4 Final 34.62 vs 34.00 (IFS 23.65 vs 22.29); Claude-Opus-4 34.13 vs 33.33 (IFS 23.61 vs 21.83); Gemini-2.5-Pro 30.36 vs 30.31 (IFS 21.65 vs 20.51). But they lower VFS in all three pairs: 60.20 vs 61.34; 58.67 vs 60.18; 50.67 vs 53.18 — [V] (p. 8, p. 9). [A] The authors describe the gains as "Consistent but Moderate" (p. 9); this goes beyond the data, given the VFS drops and the Gemini Final difference of 0.05 points.
65	5. Final Score drops sharply from static L1 tasks to interactive ones: GPT-5 61.85 on L1 vs 35.43 / 35.12 / 25.26 on L2 / L3 / L4 — [V] (p. 17). L1 is the highest category for every model, but L2 and L3 are similar and their order varies by model (e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 31.04 vs 32.86; Claude-Opus-4 (thinking) 31.52 vs 32.57; GPT-4.1 30.32 vs 31.98) — [V] (p. 17). By visual category, Final Score is lowest on data-dense layouts (GPT-5 26.05 on V4 vs 44.77 on V1), with V3 above V2 (43.77 vs 30.73) — [V] (p. 18). By domain, Life & Community is the weakest and Entertainment & Media the strongest (GPT-5 22.80 vs 47.24) — [V] (p. 19). All three category tables report Final Score only, not IFS or VFS (p. 16). So they do not show whether functional or visual fidelity drives the differences. [I] The robust contrast is L1 vs the rest; strata are small (about 9 L1 and 12 L4 tasks, see §9).
66	6. Judge reliability: three PhD students watched the agent run on 100 random generated pages; agent evaluation failed in only three cases (ambiguous element descriptors), which were then fixed — [V] (p. 9).
67	7. Case studies show distinct failure points, e.g. a model completing filter and sort but failing "add to cart"; a model failing to merge tiles in a 2048 rebuild; missing first-step elements blocking all later actions — [V] (p. 19-21).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- Not reported: the paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section (checked pp. 1-21). Design notes and disclosures that are not limitations (alternative weighting rejected, p. 7; agent-evaluation errors fixed, p. 9; LLM-assisted editing, p. 21) are recorded in Analyst notes.
71	
72	## 9. Limitations we identified
73	- [I] **IFS and VFS are not comparable in scale.** VFS averages only over checkpoints that were "successfully reached" (p. 7). It therefore cannot be lowered by functional failures that block later states. IFS divides successful actions by all actions in the trajectory (p. 7). Part of the IFS < VFS gap is therefore a property of the metrics, not only of the models. The authors mention unreachable states only to justify alpha = 0.7 (p. 7). How VFS is scored for a task where no visual checkpoint is reached is not reported. This weakens the headline "visual is solved better than function" reading. It does not weaken the finding that IFS is low in absolute terms.
74	- [I] **No code-quality or maintainability measurement.** The task forces a single self-contained HTML file with no libraries (p. 20), and only behaviour and appearance are scored. The benchmark therefore says nothing about code structure, readability or maintainability (our RQ3), and the single-file format is far from how real apps are built.
75	- [I] **Judge overlap.** Gemini-2.5-Pro is both the assertion/visual judge (p. 7) and one of the evaluated models (p. 8). Self-preference bias is not tested; its mid-table rank makes a large bias unlikely, but it is not ruled out.
76	- [I] **Moderate human alignment, tuned in-sample.** The weights were chosen to maximise rho on the same 60 instances used to report rho = 0.57 / 0.65 (p. 17); there is no held-out check. These are moderate correlations, so the Final Score is only partly aligned with human judgement. Agreement among the five raters is not reported (p. 17). The same is true of agreement among the three PhD students who observed the agent (p. 9).
77	- [I] **Evaluator re-scoring after fixes unclear.** The 3/100 agent failures were "rectified" (p. 9). Whether all 28 x 113 evaluations were re-run after the fixes is not reported. Element resolution from natural-language descriptions (p. 17) may itself involve a model, so the "deterministic" label (p. 6) is an author claim we cannot check.
78	- [I] **No variance reporting.** Single point estimates with default sampling settings (p. 8) and no repeated runs reported; several model gaps are tiny (e.g. 30.36 vs 30.31, p. 9) and could be noise.
79	- [I] **Unclear failure propagation.** It is not stated whether a failed early action stops the replay or whether later actions are still attempted (p. 7); Case 4 suggests failures cascade (p. 21). This affects how IFS should be read.
80	- [I] **Possible contamination.** Tasks come from popular live websites (e.g. an IMDb mock in Figure 2, p. 2); models may have seen similar code in training. Asset anonymisation (p. 5) reduces name cues but not memorised page structure. Not discussed by the authors.
81	- [I] **Small strata.** L1 (about 9 tasks) and L4 (about 12 tasks), derived by us from the percentages on p. 3, give unstable per-category scores.
82	
83	## 10. Threats to validity
84	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Task filtering removed "overly trivial" and "disputed" tasks without stated criteria (p. 6), which may shift difficulty. All models get identical inputs and prompt (p. 18), which supports a fair comparison. Video downsampling to at most 64 frames (p. 8) may remove interaction evidence from long videos (max 172.9 s, p. 6); this affects all models equally but penalises long tasks.
85	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Front-end only, one HTML file, mocked backend (p. 20); 113 tasks. Results do not transfer directly to multi-file apps, backends, or native desktop/mobile apps.
86	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] IFS measures replay of one ground-truth trajectory, not general behavioural equivalence; VFS mixes OCR, DINO and an MLLM rubric in which text content carries 40 of 100 points (p. 20). Both are proxies for "functional fidelity" and "visual fidelity". They also use different denominators: VFS covers only reached checkpoints, IFS all actions (p. 7). So the size of the IFS-VFS gap is partly metric-induced and should not be read as a direct comparison of the two capabilities. The fixed alpha = 0.7 encodes a value judgement (functionality matters more), supported only by rho = 0.65 (p. 17).
87	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs, tests or repeated runs (p. 8-9); conclusions about small differences (thinking vs non-thinking) are not statistically supported.
88	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts are published in the appendix (p. 20-21) and data and code are promised (p. 1). Proprietary model versions, default sampling settings and a proprietary judge model (p. 7) limit exact reproduction.
89	
90	## 11. Future research directions
91	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9): focus on "temporal reasoning, dynamic asset binding, and robust code synthesis"; structured code generation and state management as key directions (p. 9).
92	- Suggested by us [I]: (a) add code-quality/maintainability measures (static analysis, modularity) to IWR-style tasks so fidelity and code quality are measured together (our RQ5); (b) allow multi-file or framework-based outputs and agentic, iterative generation; (c) report repeated runs with variance and a held-out human-alignment set; (d) use a judge model that is not also evaluated.
93	
94	## 12. Relevance to our research
95	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirectly). Not RQ3.
96	- How it informs our work [I]: IWR-Bench is a direct example of AI "reverse engineering" an application from observable behaviour (a video) rather than from a written spec, so it fits RQ1. Its main result is central evidence for RQ2: functional correctness is low for every model (IFS < 25), and IFS sits far below VFS. The size of that gap is partly a product of how VFS is defined (only reached checkpoints, see §9). Its metric design (action replay with an agent judge, visual composite, human-calibrated weights) and weaknesses (no variance, in-sample calibration, judge overlap) inform RQ4 and our own study design. It illustrates the gap behind RQ5: fidelity is measured, but code quality and maintainability are not. [I] The result is directionally consistent with [@bai2026recreationworld], which finds static structure reproduced better than action-conditioned behaviour within its programmatic tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16-17]. However, bai's visual channel is not higher than its programmatic channel in aggregate [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11]. The two papers measure the gap differently, and here the gap is partly metric-induced (see §9). The convergence supports "static structure is easier than interaction logic". It does not support "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity".

29	## 1. Research objective
30	- [A] Evaluate coding agents on "reference-guided" software engineering: inferring intended behaviour by interacting with a working web application, then implementing it in an incomplete or empty application. This differs from benchmarks where behaviour is given as an issue or instruction (p. 1).
31	- [A] Turn working interactive web apps into a scalable, automatically built source of verifiable tasks ("application-to-task factorization") with controllable difficulty ("restoration depth") (p. 2).
32	
33	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
34	- Not stated as formal RQs. [A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). [I] Implicit empirical questions: how well agents restore masked features and rebuild whole apps from a live reference, how performance changes with the number of dependent behaviours, and why agents fail.
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
38	- Approach / model / intervention:
39	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
40	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
42	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
43	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
45	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
46	
47	## 4. Dataset and sample
48	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
49	- Sample size (N) and unit:
50	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
52	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
53	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
54	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
55	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
56	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
