58	## 5. Experimental setup
59	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
60	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
61	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
62	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
63	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
64	- [V] Number of runs, full reconstruction: 36 runs = 12 apps x 3 models (p. 11; p. 12). [I] Partial reconstruction: the number of runs per task is not stated. No variance is reported, so presumably one run each. Repeats or seeds: not reported.
65	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
66	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
67	
68	## 6. Evaluation metrics
69	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
70	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
71	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
72	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
73	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
74	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
75	
76	## 7. Key findings
77	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
78	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
79	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
80	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
81	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
82	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
83	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
84	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
85	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
86	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).

88	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
89	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
90	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
91	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
92	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
93	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
94	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
95	
96	## 9. Limitations we identified
97	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry, with application state kept in `context.state` "so the verifier can reset it" (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
98	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
99	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
100	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
101	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
102	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
103	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
104	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
105	- [I] The abstract places the full-reconstruction results under "Across nine frontier coding agents" (p. 1; same wording p. 2), but only 3 models were evaluated in that setting (p. 11). Synthesis should not describe 49.2% as best-of-nine.
106	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: apparently one run per cell (runs per task not stated for partial reconstruction), full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
107	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
108	
109	## 10. Threats to validity
110	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
111	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
112	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
113	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
114	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
115	
116	## 11. Future research directions
117	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
118	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
119	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
120	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
121	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
122	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
123	- Suggested by us [I]:
124	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
125	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
126	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
127	  4. Add repeated runs.
128	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
129	
130	## 12. Relevance to our research
131	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
132	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Measure whether software-engineering (SWE) agents can develop whole programs "holistically", including the high-level architecture decisions that existing bug-fix or single-feature benchmarks do not test (p. 1; p. 2).
30	- [A] Task: "given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable's behavior" (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [I] Implicit questions: (1) can LMs rebuild real programs from an executable plus docs; (2) do generated behavioural tests capture the programs well enough to judge this; (3) how do model-written codebases and development trajectories differ from human ones; (4) how often do models cheat when allowed internet access.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A benchmark built semi-automatically from open-source repositories, plus an evaluation of 9 LMs, two ablations (forced different language; internet access with cheating detection), test-suite validation (coverage, assertion strength) and descriptive analyses of codebases and trajectories (p. 3; p. 5; p. 7; p. 9).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] The agent receives the compiled gold executable (execute-only permissions, so it cannot be decompiled) and its usage documentation, inside a Docker container without internet. It must write source code in any language plus a build script that produces an executable with the same behaviour (p. 2; p. 4; p. 18). [V] The system prompt forbids obtaining source code, wrapping the binary, and decompiling or tracing it (strace/ltrace); only running the executable and reading the bundled docs is allowed (p. 19; p. 20).
38	- Fidelity oracle: [V] Behavioural tests are generated by a SWE-agent (mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5) that explores the program, its source code, existing tests and documentation. It harvests existing behavioural tests and iteratively adds tests that cover missing code paths, guided by line coverage (p. 3). Assertions target observable effects only: stdout/stderr content, exit codes and files produced (p. 2; p. 3). Weak tests are flagged by an assertion-quality linter and revised. Tests that do not pass the gold binary deterministically, or that pass a dummy binary, are discarded (p. 3; p. 27). The tests are never shown to the solving agent (p. 3).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 LMs compared with each other; no human baseline ("we do not carry out any formal human studies") (p. 5; p. 20). For test quality, the generated suites are compared with the projects' native test suites (p. 7; p. 8).
40	- [I] Relation to our topic: this is the closest design to black-box reverse engineering of an application. The agent observes the running program and its docs but not the source, and fidelity is judged by behavioural equivalence. The targets are CLI/TUI programs, not GUI or web apps.
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): [V] 200 GitHub repositories in compiled languages that build a standalone executable: Rust 107, Go 46, C/C++ 45, other 2 (one Java, one Haskell). They range from small CLI tools to FFmpeg, SQLite, DuckDB, PHP and Lua (p. 2; p. 4).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 200 tasks; 248,853 test functions (median 770 per task, min 224, max 14,645) (p. 4). [V] 9 models x 200 tasks = 1,800 runs (p. 10); some analyses use 1,788 runs (p. 32). [V] Median codebase size 8,635 code lines (min 212, max 2,701,283) and 50 code files (p. 4). [V] Difficulty bins: Easy 28, Medium 143, Hard 29 (p. 31).
45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filter for repositories that can produce a standalone executable, with compiled language as the heuristic. Repositories whose executable needs the internet are excluded; 18 networking tools are kept and tested over localhost (p. 3; p. 21). [I] How the 200 were chosen from the eligible pool (random, by stars, by build success) is not reported.
46	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code at github.com/facebookresearch/ProgramBench, open-sourced (p. 1; p. 2).
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] mini-SWE-agent (bash-only minimal scaffold), vendor-default hyperparameters, 20 CPUs and 60 GB RAM per container, 1,000-step and 6-hour limits (p. 5), 3-minute per-action timeout, no cost limit, outputs truncated at 10,000 characters (p. 32). [V] Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 with Rust 1.92.0, Python 3.12, Go 1.21.0, a C/C++ toolchain and tmux for TUIs (p. 16). [V] Binary test assets that models cannot easily generate (images, audio, custom formats) are provided; standard text formats are not (p. 21; p. 22). [V] Before evaluation, all files matching the hash of the original executable are removed, and git history is wiped (p. 18; p. 19).
50	- Number of runs: [V] One run per model-task (1,800 runs, p. 10). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
51	- Code availability: [A] public (p. 1).
52	
53	## 6. Evaluation metrics
54	- % Resolved: share of tasks where all tests pass and no cheating is flagged; the primary metric (p. 5).
55	- % Almost: share of tasks with ≥95% of tests passing (p. 6).
56	- % Tests Passed: per-task pass fraction. The authors say it is "only meaningful for relative comparisons" and "does not reliably correlate with percentage of working functionality" (p. 5).
57	- Test-suite quality: line coverage of the original binary versus native suites; dummy pass rate (share of tests that a trivially wrong program passes) (p. 7; p. 8).
58	- Code structure (descriptive): lines of code, number of files, maximum directory depth, function count and average function length, compared with the reference, for runs passing ≥75% of tests (p. 8; p. 9).
59	- Trajectory metrics: action types (read/write/probe/execute/git) classified by keyword matching; edit counts; share of code written in the single largest edit (p. 9; p. 10).
60	- Cheating rate: majority vote of 9 LM judges (p. 6; p. 17).
61	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests or confidence intervals. The paper reports Pearson correlations of pass rate with API calls (r = 0.27) and cost (r = 0.21) (p. 33) and Fleiss' κ for judge agreement (p. 17). [I] The statement that "test pass rates are significantly different between models" (p. 2) is not backed by any reported test.
62	
63	## 7. Key findings
64	1. [V] No model resolves any task (0% resolved for all 9). Claude Opus 4.7 reaches ≥95% of tests on 3.0% of tasks, Opus 4.6 on 2.5%, Sonnet 4.6 on 1.6%, and all others on 0% (p. 6).
65	2. [V] Macro-averaged test pass rates: Opus 4.6 52.0%, Opus 4.7 51.2%, Sonnet 4.6 48.5%, GPT 5.4 38.3%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.6%, down to GPT 5 mini 15.9%. Rates fall from Easy to Hard for every model, e.g. Opus 4.6 from 73.9% to 24.7% (p. 31).
66	3. [V] Across all runs, the median pass rate is 32%; about 18% of runs fall in the 0–5% bin, and fewer than 5% exceed 90% (p. 32). C/C++ tasks average 27.7%, against 38.5% for Rust and 38.4% for Go (p. 33).
67	4. [V] Generated test suites average 79.7% line coverage (median 86.2%), against 56.8% (median 64.3%) for native suites, over 100 sampled repositories. Against 12 dedicated behavioural/integration suites, coverage is 62.16% versus 66.11% (p. 7; p. 8).
68	5. [V] The assertion linter cut the mean dummy pass rate from 18.5% to 3.7%, and the stricter tests were 20–30 percentage points harder to pass without changing the model ranking (p. 8; p. 23).
69	6. [V] Models chose the reference language in exactly 50% of runs. Python was the most common choice overall (36% of 1,800 runs) (p. 8).
70	7. [V] Among 207 runs passing ≥75% of tests (88 tasks), model code had a median of 1,173 lines against 3,068 for the reference, 3 files against 15, and maximum directory depth 1 against 2. 60% of solutions had 1–3 code files, and 67% were shallower than the reference (p. 9).
71	8. [V] Models write 10–29% as many functions as the reference, and their functions are longer (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro 1.62x, Sonnet 4.6 1.46x, GPT 5.4 1.08x average length) (p. 8; p. 9).
72	9. [V] Development styles differ widely. Sonnet 4.6 issues a median of 868 commands per task, GPT 5.4 17 (p. 9). GPT 5.4 writes nearly all its code in one turn and makes 1.2 file modifications per trajectory on average, with 39.5% of trajectories making none (p. 10; p. 11). For the four models in the trajectory analysis (Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4), probing the executable is the second-largest action category, at 22.6–34.1% of turns (p. 10).
73	10. [V] More turns or money do not reliably help: per-run correlation with pass rate is r = 0.27 for API calls and r = 0.21 for cost, driven mostly by between-model differences (p. 33).
74	11. [V] Forcing a different implementation language lowered Opus 4.7 (−8.0%) and Opus 4.6 (−3.5%) but raised each GPT model by 4.2%; the share of Python rose to 51% (p. 6; p. 7).
75	12. [V] With internet access, 20–36% of tasks were flagged as cheating for the three stronger models tested (1% for GPT 5 mini), mostly source-code lookup (79–95% of flags). Judges disagreed on many tasks, with pooled Fleiss' κ = 0.57 over 786 tasks (p. 6; p. 7; p. 17).
76	
77	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
78	- [A] A finite test suite under-approximates the executable's full specification, so evaluation is a "lower bound" on correctness: passing solutions may still differ on untested inputs (p. 12; p. 3).
79	- [A] Only input-output equivalence is tested. Non-functional properties (speed, memory, disk footprint) are not, so a passing solution could be far slower or more resource-hungry (p. 12).
80	- [A] Only a single-agent baseline is evaluated; multi-agent and human-in-the-loop settings are left for future work (p. 12).
81	- [A] Distinguishing meaningful behaviour from implementation artefacts is subjective. The gold executable is treated as the complete specification, and 5 tasks are at risk of implementation-dependent output (p. 26).
82	- [A] No formal human study of feasibility; solvability is argued theoretically (Church–Turing) and from the observable, deterministic tests (p. 20).
83	- [A] Cheating detection with LM judges is unreliable, so internet access is blocked by default (p. 6; p. 19).
84	
85	## 9. Limitations we identified
86	- [I] Possible test-oracle bias. The test-writing agent had full access to the source code (p. 21) and used Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p. 3). The behaviours it chose to test may favour what a source reader finds salient, and same-family models (Claude) top the leaderboard (p. 31). The paper does not test for this.
87	- [I] "Agent-driven fuzzing" (p. 1) overstates the method. The tests are LLM-written, coverage-guided pytest cases (p. 3; p. 23), not randomised input fuzzing. Coverage is high, but semantic coverage of edge cases is unknown.
88	- [I] Contamination is only partly controlled. No-internet stops lookup, not memory. Many targets (FFmpeg, SQLite, jq, ripgrep) are famous and widely present in training data, and models can identify the program from `--help` output (p. 17). The different-language ablation (p. 5; p. 6) is the only memorisation probe, and its mixed results do not settle the question.
89	- [I] Code-quality evidence is thin. Only size and structure statistics are reported (LoC, files, depth, function count and length) (p. 9), with no maintainability index, smells, duplication, tests, documentation or readability. These are computed only on runs passing ≥75% of tests, a selected subset, and are confounded by language changes: Python rewrites of C code are naturally shorter (p. 35). "Monolithic" is shown, but whether it is worse for maintenance is not measured.
90	- [I] Single run per model-task (p. 10) with vendor-default sampling (p. 5), so run-to-run variance is unknown. Differences between closely ranked models (e.g. Opus 4.6 52.0% vs Opus 4.7 51.2%, p. 31) cannot be separated from noise.
91	- [I] Small internal inconsistencies:
92	  - 1,800 runs (p. 10) vs 1,788 runs (p. 32);
93	  - median tests per task 770 (p. 4) vs 750 (p. 23);
94	  - the Fig. 12 boxplot shows Sonnet 42% and Gemini 51%, the text says 44% and 53%, and the caption says GPT 5.4 writes "a median of 96%" while the text says 100% (p. 10);
95	  - "best model" is Opus 4.7 by % almost (p. 6), but Opus 4.6 has the higher mean pass rate (p. 31).
96	  
97	  None changes the conclusions, but they lower confidence in exact figures.
98	- [I] The main metric (% resolved) is all-or-nothing and saturates at 0% for every model (p. 6), so it cannot rank models; the paper relies on the softer metric that it itself says is only relative (p. 5).
99	- [I] Tasks are CLI/TUI programs; GUI, web or mobile apps are not covered, so UI and visual fidelity are untested.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: separate build and inference containers, execute-only binary, wiped git history, no internet, hash-based removal of the original binary (p. 18; p. 19). [I] Remaining threats: pretraining memory of famous programs; test generation by a same-family model with source access; the provided test assets may hint at tested behaviours (p. 21).
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Compiled-language CLI/TUI programs; a minimal single-agent scaffold, unlike practitioners' vibe-coding tools with rich IDE context and human steering (p. 5; p. 12).
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Behavioural equivalence on observable stdout/stderr/exit codes/files is a strong operational definition of functional fidelity for CLIs. The authors admit, however, that % tests passed does not track the share of working functionality (p. 5), and that untested inputs remain (p. 12). Code-structure metrics are size measures, not quality measures.
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] One run per cell; no CIs or tests; large N (200 tasks) partly offsets this for model-level means, but not for per-task claims.
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Harness configuration, prompts, linter rules and the full repository list are reported (p. 19; p. 27; p. 32; p. 36). [A] Benchmark open-sourced (p. 2).
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 12):
110	  - richer test generation that improves coverage and adds system constraints (speed, memory);
111	  - multi-agent approaches to long-horizon coding;
112	  - human-centred agents, where a developer guides design decisions while the agent works from the executable;
113	  - using the pipeline to generate training data (p. 5).
114	- Suggested by us [I]:
115	  1. Add maintainability measures (complexity, smells, duplication, modularity, ease of change) to the rebuilt codebases, and compare across languages.
116	  2. Repeat runs to estimate variance.
117	  3. Generate tests with several model families to check oracle bias.
118	  4. Extend the same black-box protocol to GUI/web applications, where observable behaviour includes visuals and interaction.
119	
120	## 12. Relevance to our research
121	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
122	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the most direct evidence on our core scenario: an agent rebuilding software only from the running artefact and its documentation, judged by behavioural equivalence. It gives (a) a concrete protocol for black-box reconstruction with leakage controls, (b) an oracle-construction method with measured coverage and assertion strength, and (c) evidence that rebuilds diverge structurally from human code (monolithic, few files, long functions). It does not measure maintainability as such, does not cover GUIs, and has no human-in-the-loop condition. These three gaps sit directly on RQ3 and RQ5.

18	# Design2Code: Benchmarking Multimodal Code Generation for Automated Front-End Engineering
19	
20	- Authors: Si, Chenglei; Zhang, Yanzhe; Li, Ryan; Yang, Zhengyuan; Liu, Ruibo; Yang, Diyi
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Build the first real-world benchmark for converting a webpage screenshot (visual design) directly into HTML/CSS code with multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), with automatic visual-fidelity metrics and human evaluation, and use it to compare models and prompting methods [A] (p. 1).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions: how well current MLLMs turn screenshots into code that renders into the reference page; whether text-augmented and self-revision prompting help; whether automatic metrics agree with human judgement; what makes a webpage hard [I] (based on sections 3–4, pp. 4–8).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus comparative evaluation; automatic metric evaluation on all 484 test pages, human evaluation on a 100-page sample; regression analysis of metrics against human preferences [V] (pp. 2–7).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: three prompting methods: (1) Direct prompting (screenshot + instruction to produce one HTML+CSS file); (2) Text-Augmented prompting (screenshot + all text extracted from the original page appended, to remove the OCR burden); (3) Self-Revision prompting (model sees reference screenshot, screenshot of its text-augmented output and that code, and is asked to revise) [V] (p. 4–5). Prompts explicitly say no JavaScript is needed for dynamic interactions [V] (p. 14). The authors also fine-tune their own Design2Code-18B (CogAgent-18B, LoRA rank 8, on a random 20% of WebSight v0.1) [V] (pp. 5, 15).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: commercial GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision; open models LLaVA-V1.6-Mixtral-7B, DeepSeek-VL-7B, Idefics2-8B; fine-tuned WebSight VLM-8B and Design2Code-18B [V] (p. 5). On Design2Code-HARD: GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Flash [V] (p. 8). Authors state comparisons are "not apple-to-apple" because of model size and training-data differences [A] (p. 5). Human pairwise comparisons use Gemini Pro Vision Direct as the single reference baseline [V] (p. 5).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): webpages linked from the C4 validation set; CSS embedded into one HTML file per page, giving 127.9k pages [V] (p. 2). Design2Code-HARD pages are sourced from GitHub ("Real-World (GitHub)", Table 4, p. 14) and filtered "using the same filtering process" (p. 8) [V]; how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described.
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 484 webpages (test cases) [V] (p. 3); HARD: 80 webpages [V] (p. 8). Average 31,216 GPT-2 tokens per file (min 784, max 98,637), 158 tags on average, 84 HTML5 tag types, DOM depth 13 on average [V] (p. 3). Domain annotation on a random 25% subsample (N=120): company/org 27.7%, blog 25.3%, homepage 13.3% most common [V] (p. 3).
42	- Sampling / selection method: automatic filtering (drop files >100k tokens, image-only or text-only layouts, deduplication) → 14k pages; strip external dependencies (script, iframe, svg, external links, href, media replaced by placeholders); first two authors manually curated a random 7k of the 14k for stand-alone rendering, no sensitive content and good formatting, after reaching 75% agreement on 200 jointly annotated pages → 484 pages; about one week of work [V] (pp. 2–3, 13). Diversity was sought "as possible" but no formal stratification is described [V] (p. 13).
43	- Data availability (public? link?): authors state they release the dataset under the ODC-By license [A] (p. 10); no URL is given in our PDF [V] (p. 10).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: commercial models with greedy decoding and max 4,096 new tokens; model versions gpt-4o-2024-05-13, gpt-4-1106-vision-preview, claude-3-opus-20240229, gemini-1.0-pro-vision [V] (p. 14). Open models: temperature 0.5, repetition penalty 1.1; reference and generated screenshots concatenated into one image for single-image models; Qwen-VL-Chat and Mantis excluded because they failed to produce HTML in >80% of cases [V] (pp. 14–15). Fine-tuning: batch 32, lr 1e-5, 5,000 steps, 4× A6000 for about 2 days, checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set [V] (p. 15). Gemini 1.5 is absent from the 484-page table; a footnote reports "empty responses with unexplained errors while testing Gemini 1.5" (p. 14), although Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash results appear on HARD (Table 3, p. 8) [V]. Human evaluators: Prolific, US only, ≥2,500 surveys with ≥98% pass rate, 60 participants, $16/hour, 5 annotators per item, majority vote [V] (pp. 5, 15).
47	- Code availability: authors promise "clear ethical use guidelines for all data, code, and model releases" [A] (p. 10); no repository link in our PDF — not reported.
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- High-level visual similarity — CLIP(IR, IG): cosine similarity of CLIP-ViT-B/32 embeddings of the reference and rendered screenshots after resizing to squares, with text regions in-painted (Telea) to remove text [V] (p. 3).
51	- Low-level element matching, after detecting text blocks in both screenshots (by recolouring text segments in the HTML and tracking pixels, not OCR) and matching them with the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm on text similarity (pairs with similarity <0.5 ignored; neighbouring blocks may be merged) [V] (pp. 4, 13):
52	  - Block-Match — share of total block area covered by matched blocks; unmatched (missing or hallucinated) blocks lower it — measures element recall/precision [V] (pp. 4–5).
53	  - Text — character-level Sørensen-Dice similarity of matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
54	  - Position — 1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|) of normalised block centres, averaged [V] (p. 4).
55	  - Color — CIEDE2000 perceptual colour difference of text in matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
56	  - Why chosen: text-based code similarity (edit distance, htmlBLEU) cannot judge visual result because many different codes render the same page [A] (p. 3).
57	- Human evaluation: (a) pairwise Win/Tie/Lose vs Gemini Pro Vision Direct on 100 sampled pages, priority content > layout > style; (b) direct assessment of GPT-4V self-revision outputs: "can it replace the original?" and "which is better designed?" [V] (pp. 5–6, 15–16).
58	- Validation against human judgement: logistic regression on metric differences predicting Win/Lose, 50/50 split of the 100 annotated pages, 435 pairwise annotations, 79.9% test accuracy; coefficients Block-Match 0.7429, Position 0.7605, CLIP 0.4929, Color 0.3461 (all p ≤ 0.001), Text −0.3541 (p = 0.021) [V] (p. 7). Simulated win rates from a refit linear model (text removed) correlate with human "win + tie" rates across 10 systems: Pearson r = 0.975, Kendall τ = 0.931 [V] (p. 17). Inter-annotator agreement: Fleiss' κ = 0.46 (pairwise), 0.32 (replaceability), 0.26 (which is better) [V] (p. 16).
59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): only regression coefficient p-values and correlation significance (Table 7, p < 0.05 marks) [V] (pp. 7, 15). No significance tests, confidence intervals or variance across runs for model comparisons — not reported.
60	
61	## 7. Key findings
62	1. GPT-4o is best on every automatic dimension (Direct: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4) [V] (p. 6); in human pairwise evaluation GPT-4o Direct wins 92% vs the Gemini baseline [V] (p. 7).
63	2. [A] Text-augmented prompting "increases the block-match score and text similarity score on most tested models" (p. 5). [V] Block-Match rises for 4 of 7 prompted models (e.g. GPT-4V 85.8 → 87.6; Gemini 80.2 → 84.8) but falls for GPT-4o (93.0 → 92.4), Claude 3 Opus (90.2 → 89.8) and Idefics2 (46.7 → 23.6); Text rises for all except Idefics2 (80.3 → 55.6) (Table 1, p. 6). [V] Self-revision helps GPT-4V and Claude 3 a little and does not help Gemini or open models (DeepSeek-VL self-revision collapses to Block 30.1) [V] (pp. 5–6).
64	3. Main weakness: models "mostly lag in recalling visual elements ... and generating correct layout designs" [A] (p. 1); on Design2Code-HARD, the authors state that state-of-the-art models "fail to generate 30% - 40% of the block elements" [A] (p. 8). Block-Match is an area-weighted share that also penalises hallucinated blocks (pp. 4–5), so it is not a count of missed elements [I]. [V] HARD Block-Match ranges 56.6–75.1 across configurations (GPT-4o Direct 56.6, i.e. more than 40% unmatched area) (Table 3, p. 8).
65	4. [A] Authors state that WebSight VLM-8B and Design2Code-18B "match Gemini direct prompting" (p. 6). [V] Design2Code-18B is close on Block (78.5 vs 80.2), but WebSight VLM-8B is far lower on Block (55.9) and Text (86.6 vs 94.6), though higher on CLIP (87.6 vs 84.4), Position (77.3 vs 72.3) and Color (79.4 vs 66.2) (Table 1, p. 6).
66	5. Direct assessment: 49% of GPT-4V self-revision pages judged interchangeable with the reference; generated pages preferred over the original in 64% of cases [V] (p. 6). Kappa for these questions is low (0.32, 0.26) [V] (p. 16).
67	6. Humans weight high-level layout and presence of content, not exact text: text similarity has a negative coefficient in predicting preference [V] (p. 7). Human and automatic rankings disagree in places (e.g. humans prefer WebSight VLM-8B over Design2Code-18B despite worse Block-Match/Text) [V] (pp. 6–7).
68	7. Total tag count is the strongest difficulty indicator (r = −0.28 with Block-Match for GPT-4V self-revision); non-English pages are harder [V] (pp. 8, 15).
69	8. Code quality, maintainability or functional behaviour of the generated code is not measured; all metrics are visual/textual on rendered screenshots [V] (pp. 3–4).
70	
71	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
72	- Better prompting is needed for complex pages, e.g. incremental generation of page parts [A] (p. 10).
73	- Training directly on real webpages is hard because they are long and noisy [A] (p. 10).
74	- Input is screenshot-only; Figma frames or sketches would need a re-designed evaluation [A] (p. 10).
75	- Only static webpages; dynamic pages need evaluation of "interactive functions beyond just visual similarity" [A] (p. 10).
76	- Human evaluation should not be "blindly trusted as the oracle" because of human top-down attention bias [A] (pp. 7–8).
77	- Text-block matching may be imperfect when granularity differs (non-contiguous merges not searched) [A] (p. 13).
78	
79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] Fidelity is purely visual (screenshot similarity). No functional, behavioural, or code-level quality measure (e.g. HTML validity, semantic structure, maintainability, responsiveness) — based on metric definitions pp. 3–4. For our project this means Design2Code says nothing about whether a rebuilt page works or is maintainable.
81	- [I] JavaScript, iframes, SVG and external links are stripped and prompts say no JS is needed (pp. 13–14); the task is reconstruction of a static, de-functionalised snapshot, not of an application.
82	- [I] Human validation is modest: 100 pages, Fleiss' κ only 0.46/0.32/0.26 (p. 16), logistic regression accuracy 79.9% on a 50-page test half (p. 7). The very high Pearson r = 0.975 is computed over only 10 system-level points (p. 17) and compares predicted wins with human "win + tie" — an aggregation that inflates agreement.
83	- [I] Test pages come from C4, a common pretraining corpus; data contamination is not discussed (grep for "contamin" finds nothing).
84	- [I] Single run per configuration with greedy decoding; no variance or significance testing between models (pp. 5–6, 14).
85	- [I] Design2Code-HARD pages are sourced from GitHub (p. 14) and filtered "using the same filtering process" (p. 8); how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described, so the HARD set's representativeness cannot be judged.
86	- [I] The metric-validation agreement is not out-of-sample. The logistic regression is trained on 50 of the 100 human-annotated pages (p. 7); the linear model for simulated win rates is refit "on the same training examples" and applied to "all 484 examples", which include those training pages (p. 17); and the human "win + tie" rates it is compared with come from the same 100 pages (Table 8, p. 17). So r = 0.975 / τ = 0.931 partly reflects fit on the training data, on top of being computed over only 10 system-level points.
87	- [I] Element metrics are text-anchored (blocks come from text segments, p. 13); images, icons and non-text elements are only covered by CLIP.
88	
89	## 10. Threats to validity
90	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): manual curation by the authors (selection bias towards well-formatted pages) (p. 13); possible C4 pretraining contamination (not discussed); Design2Code-18B checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set (p. 15) [I].
91	- External (generalisability of sample/context): static, single-page, English-dominant web pages with placeholders for media; HARD set of 80 (p. 8); no mobile apps, multi-page or interactive apps [I].
92	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): metrics measure visual similarity of a rendered screenshot, not functional fidelity or code quality; Text metric is negatively associated with human preference (p. 7), so the five metrics do not all point the same way [I].
93	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no CIs or tests for model differences; low-moderate inter-annotator agreement (p. 16); system-level correlation on n = 10 (p. 17), and that correlation is not an out-of-sample validation because the simulating model was fit on 50 of the same 100 annotated pages and applied to all 484 pages including them (pp. 7, 17) [I].
94	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): prompts, model versions and decoding settings reported (p. 14); fine-tuning hyper-parameters reported (p. 15); dataset release claimed but no link in our PDF (p. 10); commercial model versions may be deprecated [I].
95	
96	## 11. Future research directions
97	- Stated by authors [A]: incremental generation for complex pages; cleaning pipelines for training on real webpages; Figma/sketch inputs; dynamic webpages with interactive-function evaluation (p. 10); "generate UIs that support dynamic user interactions" (p. 9); website-design improvement tools (p. 6).
98	- Suggested by us [I]: pair the visual metrics with behavioural tests and static code-quality analysis of the generated HTML/CSS; report run-to-run variance; check pretraining contamination of C4-sourced pages.
99	
100	## 12. Relevance to our research
101	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
102	- How it informs our work [I]: Design2Code is the reference benchmark for screenshot-to-code reconstruction and the origin of the Block/Text/Position/Color/CLIP metric family reused by later work. It shows how visual fidelity can be measured and partly validated against humans, and it clearly leaves out interaction, functionality and code quality — the dimensions our project needs.

18	# Interaction2Code: Benchmarking MLLM-based Interactive Webpage Code Generation from Interactive Prototyping
19	
20	- Authors: Xiao, Jingyu; Wan, Yuxuan; Huo, Yintong; Wang, Zixin; Xu, Xinyi; Wang, Wenxuan; Xu, Zhiyao; Wang, Yuhang; Lyu, Michael R.
21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index), extracted from arXiv:2411.03292v3 (1 Mar 2026), not the ASE proceedings PDF
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Formulate the Interaction-to-Code task (generate an interactive webpage from an "interactive prototype": screenshots before and after each interaction), build a real-world benchmark for it, and systematically study how well MLLMs reproduce webpage interactions, why they fail, and how prompting can help [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- No formal RQs. The study is organised around four reported "limitations" of MLLMs: (1) worse generation of interactive parts than of the full page; (2) ten failure types; (3) poor performance on visually subtle interactions; (4) insufficient understanding from visual input alone — each paired with an improvement strategy [V] (pp. 1–2).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus empirical comparison of models and prompts; automatic evaluation via Selenium-driven interaction replay; human usability and pairwise evaluation; qualitative failure taxonomy; sub-experiments on visual saliency and input modality; ablation; small user study [V] (pp. 3–11).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: MLLM receives the original screenshot plus post-interaction screenshot(s) and must output one HTML+CSS+JavaScript file, tagging interactive elements with ids (e.g. id="interact1") so a webdriver can trigger them [V] (pp. 3–5). Prompts: Direct, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Mark (red bounding boxes on interactive areas), Failure-aware Prompt (FAP: lists the ten failure types) [V] (p. 5). Further enhancements: Visual Saliency Enhancement (crop to enlarge the interaction area) and adding human-written textual descriptions of interactions [V] (pp. 9–10).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o-20240806, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620, Qwen2.5-VL-instruct 3B/7B/72B; Direct prompting is the baseline for prompt comparisons; Gemini-1.5-flash Direct is the human pairwise baseline [V] (pp. 4, 6). No non-LLM or prior UI-to-code system (e.g. DCGen) is run as a baseline [I] (based on p. 4 model list).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): (1) C4 validation set (CommonCrawl), filtered as in Design2Code, 1,000 pages sampled across 15 topics, from which four PhD students each picked about 25 → 100 pages; (2) 27 popular GitHub projects (average 13k stars) with deployed links, found via "open-production-web-projects" and "awesome-opensource-apps", to include UI-framework pages [V] (pp. 2–3).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 127 webpages and 374 interactions; 15+ topics; 23 tag categories and 8 visual categories (31 interaction categories) [V] (pp. 1, 3). Most frequent interactive tags: button 235, input 52, span 37, link 36 [V] (p. 3).
42	- Sampling / selection method: manual selection by four PhD students for complexity (at least one meaningful interaction) and diversity; 1–10 "important and functional" interactions kept per page; trivial interactions (e.g. hover underline) excluded [V] (pp. 2–3). Selection guidelines are only in the external artifact [V] (p. 3).
43	- Data availability (public? link?): data and code at https://github.com/WebPAI/Interaction2Code [A] (p. 1).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: temperature 0; max output 4,096 tokens (commercial) and 2,048 (Qwen); other parameters default [V] (p. 4). Selenium webdriver locates elements by id, performs the interaction and screenshots the result; the changed region is extracted by pixel subtraction (same-size pages) or a Git-diff of rows/columns (size-changing pages) (Algorithm 1) [V] (p. 4). Data-contamination check: BLEU between generated and original HTML is 0.12–0.14 for the four main models [V] (p. 5). FAP experiment: 2/3 of the dataset used to derive failure types, 1/3 for testing [V] (p. 8). Saliency and modality experiments use 10 randomly sampled failure-case webpages each [V] (pp. 9–10).
47	- Code availability: GitHub repository above [A] (p. 1). Appendix H (tool) and detailed human-evaluation instructions are referenced but are not in our 13-page PDF [V] (pp. 6, 11).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Full-page metrics: CLIP score (visual similarity); SSIM (structural similarity); Text similarity = BLEU on OCR-extracted text; Widget Similarity (WS) and Widget Match Rate (WMR) computed with the GUIPilot method [V] (p. 4).
51	- Interaction-part metrics (on the extracted changed region): CLIP, SSIM, Text; Position similarity P = 1 − max(|xo − xg|, |yo − yg|) of normalised interaction-area centres; Implement Rate IR = implemented / (implemented + unimplemented), where "implemented" means detectable by the webdriver [V] (p. 4).
52	- Human metrics: Usability Rate UR = usable / (usable + unusable), judged by four PhD students (three years front-end experience) — usable if the implementation "precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype"; pairwise Win/Tie/Lose by five annotators against Gemini-1.5-flash Direct, majority (≥3) rule; failure-type annotation [V] (pp. 4, 6–7).
53	- Validation against human judgement: authors state human results "are consistent with Section V-A, confirming the validity of our automatic evaluation metrics" [A] (p. 6). No correlation coefficient, agreement statistic or regression is reported — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement for usability, pairwise or failure annotation — not reported (failure types reached by discussion to consensus on a 25% sample) [V] (p. 7). Number of items in the human evaluations — not reported.
54	- Widget metrics are acknowledged as unreliable for web pages: WS is "consistently poor" (0.02–0.05) and GUIPilot omits many elements because it was designed for mobile UIs [V] (pp. 5–6).
55	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none for model or prompt comparisons; saliency effect described as "significantly increases" without a test [V] (pp. 8–9). Not reported.
56	
57	## 7. Key findings
58	1. Interactive parts are generated worse than full pages for all models (e.g. GPT-4o average full-page CLIP 0.7059 vs interaction-part CLIP 0.5598) [V] (p. 6).
59	2. Claude-3.5-Sonnet has the best averages on most metrics (e.g. interaction IR 0.7870, full-page Text 0.5835); GPT-4o with Mark prompt has the highest single IR (0.8128); Qwen2.5-VL-72B ≈ Gemini-1.5-flash; performance rises with model size [V] (pp. 5–6).
60	3. Human Usability Rate (Fig. 6a, read from figure labels): GPT-4o Direct/CoT/Mark 73/74/81%; Claude 66/69/77%; Gemini 47/53/64%; Qwen-72B 41/43/54%; Qwen-3B 17–19% [V] (p. 6). Mark prompting gives the largest usability gain (Claude +11 points vs Direct) [V] (p. 6).
61	4. Ten failure types in two groups (interactive element: missing, no interaction, wrong element, wrong type, wrong position; interaction effects: wrong position, wrong type, effect on wrong element, partial implementation, wrong function) [V] (pp. 7–8). Failures (a) missing element, (b) no interaction and (j) wrong function have usability <10% (0%, 6.93%, 0%) [V] (pp. 7–8). Main failure modes are "No interaction", "Partial implementation", "Interactive element missing" and "Wrong function" [A] (p. 8).
62	5. Failures cluster into spatial (a, c, e, f), type (d, g) and behavioural (b, h, i, j) failures [A] (p. 8).
63	6. Low visual saliency (small interaction area) lowers SSIM and position similarity; cropping to enlarge the area (1.2–3×) recovers interactions on 10 failure pages [V] (pp. 9–10).
64	7. Authors state that combined visual + text input "consistently outperforms single-modality inputs across all prompt types" [A] (p. 10). On 10 failure pages with GPT-4o, V+T is best on most cells (e.g. Direct: Position 0.7157 V+T vs 0.3951 V) [V] (p. 10), but not all: under the Mark prompt, SSIM for V+T is 0.4336, below V (0.4520) and T (0.4454) [V] (p. 10). All four enhancements combined give the best ablation result (GPT-4o interaction CLIP 0.6937 vs 0.5700) [V] (p. 11).
65	8. FAP: authors claim it improves "all models" [A] (p. 8), but Table VI shows Qwen2.5-VL-3B drops on 7 of 8 metrics and Qwen-7B on 5 of 8 [V] (p. 9).
66	9. User study: with the tool, 4 tasks took 279 s vs 413 s on average and expert similarity rating 4.5 vs 3.875 (two participants per condition, two raters) [V] (p. 11).
67	10. Code quality or maintainability of the generated HTML/CSS/JS is not measured; the only code-level measure is BLEU against the original HTML, used as a contamination check [V] (pp. 4–5).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- Limited context length: complex pages with many interactions may exceed the context window; iterative generation suggested [A] (p. 11).
71	- Model selection: only three main commercial MLLMs tested; others (e.g. Pixtral) left for future work [A] (p. 11).
72	- Back-end interactions (login, search) cannot be evaluated because the benchmark has no back-end code [A] (p. 11).
73	- Existing widget-consistency methods are designed for mobile UIs and miss web elements [A] (p. 5).
74	
75	## 9. Limitations we identified
76	- [I] Validation of automatic metrics against humans is only a qualitative "consistent" statement (p. 6); no correlation, agreement (kappa) or item counts are given. The automatic metrics are therefore not shown to measure functional fidelity.
77	- [I] "Implement Rate" counts an interaction as implemented if the webdriver can find and trigger the element (p. 4) — this measures presence, not correct behaviour; functional correctness rests on the human Usability Rate alone.
78	- [I] Interaction fidelity is judged on screenshots of state changes, not on behavioural traces or DOM/state assertions; non-visual effects (data, network, storage) are out of scope (based on pp. 3–4, 11).
79	- [I] Several sub-experiments use only 10 pages (pp. 9–10) and the user study has 2 participants per condition (p. 11); these results are anecdotal.
80	- [I] The FAP claim ("improve ... on all models", p. 8) contradicts the paper's own Table VI (p. 9) for the two smaller Qwen models.
81	- [I] Similarly, the modality claim that V+T "consistently outperforms" single modalities "across all prompt types" (p. 10) is contradicted by Table VIII for SSIM under the Mark prompt (V+T 0.4336 < V 0.4520 and T 0.4454, p. 10), and rests on only 10 pages.
82	- [I] The FAP test uses failure types derived from 2/3 of the same dataset (p. 8); split procedure and whether it is by page or by interaction is not stated.
83	- [I] Fig. 9 "No failure" shares (about 36% for GPT-4o, about 40% for Claude, read from the figure, p. 9) look hard to reconcile with Usability Rates of 73–81% (p. 6); the denominators/definitions are not explained.
84	- [I] The contamination argument (C4 has only text; BLEU 0.12–0.14, p. 5) is weak: C4 URLs' HTML is widely crawled elsewhere, and low BLEU does not rule out memorised layout.
85	- [I] No code-quality, maintainability or code-structure measurement, despite generating JavaScript event logic.
86	
87	## 10. Threats to validity
88	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): pages and interactions hand-picked by the authors' annotators (pp. 2–3); FAP failure types derived from the same benchmark (p. 8); Table VI direct baselines differ from Table IV (different subset), so improvements are relative to a subset [I].
89	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 127 pages, front-end only, no back-end; mostly click-type interactions on buttons (235 of tagged elements) (p. 3); single-file output, not multi-file framework projects [I].
90	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): visual metrics on changed regions approximate interaction fidelity; IR measures element presence; widget metrics admitted unreliable for web (p. 5) [I].
91	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single deterministic run (temperature 0); no tests, CIs or agreement statistics; small N in sub-studies [I].
92	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and code released (p. 1); prompts shown (p. 5); key guidelines and appendix only in the artifact; the PDF is arXiv v3 (1 Mar 2026), the ASE 2025 version may differ [I].
93	
94	## 11. Future research directions
95	- Stated by authors [A]: iterative multi-round generation for many interactions; testing more MLLMs (e.g. Pixtral) (p. 11); handling interactions that require back-end code (p. 11); designing widget-level consistency detection suited to web pages (pp. 5–6).
96	- Suggested by us [I]: validate interaction metrics against human usability with reported correlations; add behavioural assertions (DOM state, event sequences) and code-quality/maintainability analysis of generated JS; extend to multi-page apps with back-end.
97	
98	## 12. Relevance to our research
99	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
100	- How it informs our work [I]: this is the closest web benchmark to reverse engineering from observable behaviour: input is before/after screenshots of interactions, and the target is a page that reproduces that behaviour. It supplies a usable failure taxonomy and the Usability Rate as a human functional-fidelity measure, but its automatic metrics are weakly validated and it ignores code quality.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Measure whether software-engineering (SWE) agents can develop whole programs "holistically", including the high-level architecture decisions that existing bug-fix or single-feature benchmarks do not test (p. 1; p. 2).
30	- [A] Task: "given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable's behavior" (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [I] Implicit questions: (1) can LMs rebuild real programs from an executable plus docs; (2) do generated behavioural tests capture the programs well enough to judge this; (3) how do model-written codebases and development trajectories differ from human ones; (4) how often do models cheat when allowed internet access.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A benchmark built semi-automatically from open-source repositories, plus an evaluation of 9 LMs, two ablations (forced different language; internet access with cheating detection), test-suite validation (coverage, assertion strength) and descriptive analyses of codebases and trajectories (p. 3; p. 5; p. 7; p. 9).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] The agent receives the compiled gold executable (execute-only permissions, so it cannot be decompiled) and its usage documentation, inside a Docker container without internet. It must write source code in any language plus a build script that produces an executable with the same behaviour (p. 2; p. 4; p. 18). [V] The system prompt forbids obtaining source code, wrapping the binary, and decompiling or tracing it (strace/ltrace); only running the executable and reading the bundled docs is allowed (p. 19; p. 20).
38	- Fidelity oracle: [V] Behavioural tests are generated by a SWE-agent (mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5) that explores the program, its source code, existing tests and documentation. It harvests existing behavioural tests and iteratively adds tests that cover missing code paths, guided by line coverage (p. 3). Assertions target observable effects only: stdout/stderr content, exit codes and files produced (p. 2; p. 3). Weak tests are flagged by an assertion-quality linter and revised. Tests that do not pass the gold binary deterministically, or that pass a dummy binary, are discarded (p. 3; p. 27). The tests are never shown to the solving agent (p. 3).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 LMs compared with each other; no human baseline ("we do not carry out any formal human studies") (p. 5; p. 20). For test quality, the generated suites are compared with the projects' native test suites (p. 7; p. 8).
40	- [I] Relation to our topic: this is the closest design to black-box reverse engineering of an application. The agent observes the running program and its docs but not the source, and fidelity is judged by behavioural equivalence. The targets are CLI/TUI programs, not GUI or web apps.
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): [V] 200 GitHub repositories in compiled languages that build a standalone executable: Rust 107, Go 46, C/C++ 45, other 2 (one Java, one Haskell). They range from small CLI tools to FFmpeg, SQLite, DuckDB, PHP and Lua (p. 2; p. 4).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 200 tasks; 248,853 test functions (median 770 per task, min 224, max 14,645) (p. 4). [V] 9 models x 200 tasks = 1,800 runs (p. 10); some analyses use 1,788 runs (p. 32). [V] Median codebase size 8,635 code lines (min 212, max 2,701,283) and 50 code files (p. 4). [V] Difficulty bins: Easy 28, Medium 143, Hard 29 (p. 31).
45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Filter for repositories that can produce a standalone executable, with compiled language as the heuristic. Repositories whose executable needs the internet are excluded; 18 networking tools are kept and tested over localhost (p. 3; p. 21). [I] How the 200 were chosen from the eligible pool (random, by stars, by build success) is not reported.
46	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code at github.com/facebookresearch/ProgramBench, open-sourced (p. 1; p. 2).
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] mini-SWE-agent (bash-only minimal scaffold), vendor-default hyperparameters, 20 CPUs and 60 GB RAM per container, 1,000-step and 6-hour limits (p. 5), 3-minute per-action timeout, no cost limit, outputs truncated at 10,000 characters (p. 32). [V] Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 with Rust 1.92.0, Python 3.12, Go 1.21.0, a C/C++ toolchain and tmux for TUIs (p. 16). [V] Binary test assets that models cannot easily generate (images, audio, custom formats) are provided; standard text formats are not (p. 21; p. 22). [V] Before evaluation, all files matching the hash of the original executable are removed, and git history is wiped (p. 18; p. 19).
50	- Number of runs: [V] One run per model-task (1,800 runs, p. 10). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
51	- Code availability: [A] public (p. 1).
52	
53	## 6. Evaluation metrics
54	- % Resolved: share of tasks where all tests pass and no cheating is flagged; the primary metric (p. 5).
55	- % Almost: share of tasks with ≥95% of tests passing (p. 6).
56	- % Tests Passed: per-task pass fraction. The authors say it is "only meaningful for relative comparisons" and "does not reliably correlate with percentage of working functionality" (p. 5).
57	- Test-suite quality: line coverage of the original binary versus native suites; dummy pass rate (share of tests that a trivially wrong program passes) (p. 7; p. 8).
58	- Code structure (descriptive): lines of code, number of files, maximum directory depth, function count and average function length, compared with the reference, for runs passing ≥75% of tests (p. 8; p. 9).
59	- Trajectory metrics: action types (read/write/probe/execute/git) classified by keyword matching; edit counts; share of code written in the single largest edit (p. 9; p. 10).
60	- Cheating rate: majority vote of 9 LM judges (p. 6; p. 17).
61	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests or confidence intervals. The paper reports Pearson correlations of pass rate with API calls (r = 0.27) and cost (r = 0.21) (p. 33) and Fleiss' κ for judge agreement (p. 17). [I] The statement that "test pass rates are significantly different between models" (p. 2) is not backed by any reported test.
62	
63	## 7. Key findings
64	1. [V] No model resolves any task (0% resolved for all 9). Claude Opus 4.7 reaches ≥95% of tests on 3.0% of tasks, Opus 4.6 on 2.5%, Sonnet 4.6 on 1.6%, and all others on 0% (p. 6).
65	2. [V] Macro-averaged test pass rates: Opus 4.6 52.0%, Opus 4.7 51.2%, Sonnet 4.6 48.5%, GPT 5.4 38.3%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.6%, down to GPT 5 mini 15.9%. Rates fall from Easy to Hard for every model, e.g. Opus 4.6 from 73.9% to 24.7% (p. 31).
66	3. [V] Across all runs, the median pass rate is 32%; about 18% of runs fall in the 0–5% bin, and fewer than 5% exceed 90% (p. 32). C/C++ tasks average 27.7%, against 38.5% for Rust and 38.4% for Go (p. 33).
67	4. [V] Generated test suites average 79.7% line coverage (median 86.2%), against 56.8% (median 64.3%) for native suites, over 100 sampled repositories. Against 12 dedicated behavioural/integration suites, coverage is 62.16% versus 66.11% (p. 7; p. 8).
68	5. [V] The assertion linter cut the mean dummy pass rate from 18.5% to 3.7%, and the stricter tests were 20–30 percentage points harder to pass without changing the model ranking (p. 8; p. 23).
69	6. [V] Models chose the reference language in exactly 50% of runs. Python was the most common choice overall (36% of 1,800 runs) (p. 8).
70	7. [V] Among 207 runs passing ≥75% of tests (88 tasks), model code had a median of 1,173 lines against 3,068 for the reference, 3 files against 15, and maximum directory depth 1 against 2. 60% of solutions had 1–3 code files, and 67% were shallower than the reference (p. 9).
71	8. [V] Models write 10–29% as many functions as the reference, and their functions are longer (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro 1.62x, Sonnet 4.6 1.46x, GPT 5.4 1.08x average length) (p. 8; p. 9).
72	9. [V] Development styles differ widely. Sonnet 4.6 issues a median of 868 commands per task, GPT 5.4 17 (p. 9). GPT 5.4 writes nearly all its code in one turn and makes 1.2 file modifications per trajectory on average, with 39.5% of trajectories making none (p. 10; p. 11). For the four models in the trajectory analysis (Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4), probing the executable is the second-largest action category, at 22.6–34.1% of turns (p. 10).
73	10. [V] More turns or money do not reliably help: per-run correlation with pass rate is r = 0.27 for API calls and r = 0.21 for cost, driven mostly by between-model differences (p. 33).
74	11. [V] Forcing a different implementation language lowered Opus 4.7 (−8.0%) and Opus 4.6 (−3.5%) but raised each GPT model by 4.2%; the share of Python rose to 51% (p. 6; p. 7).
75	12. [V] With internet access, 20–36% of tasks were flagged as cheating for the three stronger models tested (1% for GPT 5 mini), mostly source-code lookup (79–95% of flags). Judges disagreed on many tasks, with pooled Fleiss' κ = 0.57 over 786 tasks (p. 6; p. 7; p. 17).
76	
77	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
78	- [A] A finite test suite under-approximates the executable's full specification, so evaluation is a "lower bound" on correctness: passing solutions may still differ on untested inputs (p. 12; p. 3).
79	- [A] Only input-output equivalence is tested. Non-functional properties (speed, memory, disk footprint) are not, so a passing solution could be far slower or more resource-hungry (p. 12).
80	- [A] Only a single-agent baseline is evaluated; multi-agent and human-in-the-loop settings are left for future work (p. 12).
81	- [A] Distinguishing meaningful behaviour from implementation artefacts is subjective. The gold executable is treated as the complete specification, and 5 tasks are at risk of implementation-dependent output (p. 26).
82	- [A] No formal human study of feasibility; solvability is argued theoretically (Church–Turing) and from the observable, deterministic tests (p. 20).
83	- [A] Cheating detection with LM judges is unreliable, so internet access is blocked by default (p. 6; p. 19).
84	
85	## 9. Limitations we identified
86	- [I] Possible test-oracle bias. The test-writing agent had full access to the source code (p. 21) and used Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p. 3). The behaviours it chose to test may favour what a source reader finds salient, and same-family models (Claude) top the leaderboard (p. 31). The paper does not test for this.
87	- [I] "Agent-driven fuzzing" (p. 1) overstates the method. The tests are LLM-written, coverage-guided pytest cases (p. 3; p. 23), not randomised input fuzzing. Coverage is high, but semantic coverage of edge cases is unknown.
88	- [I] Contamination is only partly controlled. No-internet stops lookup, not memory. Many targets (FFmpeg, SQLite, jq, ripgrep) are famous and widely present in training data, and models can identify the program from `--help` output (p. 17). The different-language ablation (p. 5; p. 6) is the only memorisation probe, and its mixed results do not settle the question.
89	- [I] Code-quality evidence is thin. Only size and structure statistics are reported (LoC, files, depth, function count and length) (p. 9), with no maintainability index, smells, duplication, tests, documentation or readability. These are computed only on runs passing ≥75% of tests, a selected subset, and are confounded by language changes: Python rewrites of C code are naturally shorter (p. 35). "Monolithic" is shown, but whether it is worse for maintenance is not measured.
90	- [I] Single run per model-task (p. 10) with vendor-default sampling (p. 5), so run-to-run variance is unknown. Differences between closely ranked models (e.g. Opus 4.6 52.0% vs Opus 4.7 51.2%, p. 31) cannot be separated from noise.
91	- [I] Small internal inconsistencies:
92	  - 1,800 runs (p. 10) vs 1,788 runs (p. 32);
93	  - median tests per task 770 (p. 4) vs 750 (p. 23);
94	  - the Fig. 12 boxplot shows Sonnet 42% and Gemini 51%, the text says 44% and 53%, and the caption says GPT 5.4 writes "a median of 96%" while the text says 100% (p. 10);
95	  - "best model" is Opus 4.7 by % almost (p. 6), but Opus 4.6 has the higher mean pass rate (p. 31).
96	  
97	  None changes the conclusions, but they lower confidence in exact figures.
98	- [I] The main metric (% resolved) is all-or-nothing and saturates at 0% for every model (p. 6), so it cannot rank models; the paper relies on the softer metric that it itself says is only relative (p. 5).
99	- [I] Tasks are CLI/TUI programs; GUI, web or mobile apps are not covered, so UI and visual fidelity are untested.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: separate build and inference containers, execute-only binary, wiped git history, no internet, hash-based removal of the original binary (p. 18; p. 19). [I] Remaining threats: pretraining memory of famous programs; test generation by a same-family model with source access; the provided test assets may hint at tested behaviours (p. 21).
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Compiled-language CLI/TUI programs; a minimal single-agent scaffold, unlike practitioners' vibe-coding tools with rich IDE context and human steering (p. 5; p. 12).
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Behavioural equivalence on observable stdout/stderr/exit codes/files is a strong operational definition of functional fidelity for CLIs. The authors admit, however, that % tests passed does not track the share of working functionality (p. 5), and that untested inputs remain (p. 12). Code-structure metrics are size measures, not quality measures.
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] One run per cell; no CIs or tests; large N (200 tasks) partly offsets this for model-level means, but not for per-task claims.
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Harness configuration, prompts, linter rules and the full repository list are reported (p. 19; p. 27; p. 32; p. 36). [A] Benchmark open-sourced (p. 2).
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 12):
110	  - richer test generation that improves coverage and adds system constraints (speed, memory);
111	  - multi-agent approaches to long-horizon coding;
112	  - human-centred agents, where a developer guides design decisions while the agent works from the executable;
113	  - using the pipeline to generate training data (p. 5).
114	- Suggested by us [I]:
115	  1. Add maintainability measures (complexity, smells, duplication, modularity, ease of change) to the rebuilt codebases, and compare across languages.
116	  2. Repeat runs to estimate variance.
117	  3. Generate tests with several model families to check oracle bias.
118	  4. Extend the same black-box protocol to GUI/web applications, where observable behaviour includes visuals and interaction.
119	
120	## 12. Relevance to our research
121	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
122	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the most direct evidence on our core scenario: an agent rebuilding software only from the running artefact and its documentation, judged by behavioural equivalence. It gives (a) a concrete protocol for black-box reconstruction with leakage controls, (b) an oracle-construction method with measured coverage and assertion strength, and (c) evidence that rebuilds diverge structurally from human code (monolithic, few files, long functions). It does not measure maintainability as such, does not cover GUIs, and has no human-in-the-loop condition. These three gaps sit directly on RQ3 and RQ5.

18	# Design2Code: Benchmarking Multimodal Code Generation for Automated Front-End Engineering
19	
20	- Authors: Si, Chenglei; Zhang, Yanzhe; Li, Ryan; Yang, Zhengyuan; Liu, Ruibo; Yang, Diyi
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
