27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Build the first real-world benchmark for converting a webpage screenshot (visual design) directly into HTML/CSS code with multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), with automatic visual-fidelity metrics and human evaluation, and use it to compare models and prompting methods [A] (p. 1).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Implicit questions: how well current MLLMs turn screenshots into code that renders into the reference page; whether text-augmented and self-revision prompting help; whether automatic metrics agree with human judgement; what makes a webpage hard [I] (based on sections 3–4, pp. 4–8).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus comparative evaluation; automatic metric evaluation on all 484 test pages, human evaluation on a 100-page sample; regression analysis of metrics against human preferences [V] (pp. 2–7).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: three prompting methods: (1) Direct prompting (screenshot + instruction to produce one HTML+CSS file); (2) Text-Augmented prompting (screenshot + all text extracted from the original page appended, to remove the OCR burden); (3) Self-Revision prompting (model sees reference screenshot, screenshot of its text-augmented output and that code, and is asked to revise) [V] (p. 4–5). Prompts explicitly say no JavaScript is needed for dynamic interactions [V] (p. 14). The authors also fine-tune their own Design2Code-18B (CogAgent-18B, LoRA rank 8, on a random 20% of WebSight v0.1) [V] (pp. 5, 15).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: commercial GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision; open models LLaVA-V1.6-Mixtral-7B, DeepSeek-VL-7B, Idefics2-8B; fine-tuned WebSight VLM-8B and Design2Code-18B [V] (p. 5). On Design2Code-HARD: GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Flash [V] (p. 8). Authors state comparisons are "not apple-to-apple" because of model size and training-data differences [A] (p. 5). Human pairwise comparisons use Gemini Pro Vision Direct as the single reference baseline [V] (p. 5).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): webpages linked from the C4 validation set; CSS embedded into one HTML file per page, giving 127.9k pages [V] (p. 2). Design2Code-HARD pages are sourced from GitHub ("Real-World (GitHub)", Table 4, p. 14) and filtered "using the same filtering process" (p. 8) [V]; how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described.
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 484 webpages (test cases) [V] (p. 3); HARD: 80 webpages [V] (p. 8). Average 31,216 GPT-2 tokens per file (min 784, max 98,637), 158 tags on average, 84 HTML5 tag types, DOM depth 13 on average [V] (p. 3). Domain annotation on a random 25% subsample (N=120): company/org 27.7%, blog 25.3%, homepage 13.3% most common [V] (p. 3).
42	- Sampling / selection method: automatic filtering (drop files >100k tokens, image-only or text-only layouts, deduplication) → 14k pages; strip external dependencies (script, iframe, svg, external links, href, media replaced by placeholders); first two authors manually curated a random 7k of the 14k for stand-alone rendering, no sensitive content and good formatting, after reaching 75% agreement on 200 jointly annotated pages → 484 pages; about one week of work [V] (pp. 2–3, 13). Diversity was sought "as possible" but no formal stratification is described [V] (p. 13).
43	- Data availability (public? link?): authors state they release the dataset under the ODC-By license [A] (p. 10); no URL is given in our PDF [V] (p. 10).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: commercial models with greedy decoding and max 4,096 new tokens; model versions gpt-4o-2024-05-13, gpt-4-1106-vision-preview, claude-3-opus-20240229, gemini-1.0-pro-vision [V] (p. 14). Open models: temperature 0.5, repetition penalty 1.1; reference and generated screenshots concatenated into one image for single-image models; Qwen-VL-Chat and Mantis excluded because they failed to produce HTML in >80% of cases [V] (pp. 14–15). Fine-tuning: batch 32, lr 1e-5, 5,000 steps, 4× A6000 for about 2 days, checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set [V] (p. 15). Gemini 1.5 is absent from the 484-page table; a footnote reports "empty responses with unexplained errors while testing Gemini 1.5" (p. 14), although Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash results appear on HARD (Table 3, p. 8) [V]. Human evaluators: Prolific, US only, ≥2,500 surveys with ≥98% pass rate, 60 participants, $16/hour, 5 annotators per item, majority vote [V] (pp. 5, 15).
47	- Code availability: authors promise "clear ethical use guidelines for all data, code, and model releases" [A] (p. 10); no repository link in our PDF — not reported.
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- High-level visual similarity — CLIP(IR, IG): cosine similarity of CLIP-ViT-B/32 embeddings of the reference and rendered screenshots after resizing to squares, with text regions in-painted (Telea) to remove text [V] (p. 3).
51	- Low-level element matching, after detecting text blocks in both screenshots (by recolouring text segments in the HTML and tracking pixels, not OCR) and matching them with the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm on text similarity (pairs with similarity <0.5 ignored; neighbouring blocks may be merged) [V] (pp. 4, 13):
52	  - Block-Match — share of total block area covered by matched blocks; unmatched (missing or hallucinated) blocks lower it — measures element recall/precision [V] (pp. 4–5).
53	  - Text — character-level Sørensen-Dice similarity of matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
54	  - Position — 1 − max(|Δx|, |Δy|) of normalised block centres, averaged [V] (p. 4).
55	  - Color — CIEDE2000 perceptual colour difference of text in matched blocks, averaged [V] (p. 4).
56	  - Why chosen: text-based code similarity (edit distance, htmlBLEU) cannot judge visual result because many different codes render the same page [A] (p. 3).
57	- Human evaluation: (a) pairwise Win/Tie/Lose vs Gemini Pro Vision Direct on 100 sampled pages, priority content > layout > style; (b) direct assessment of GPT-4V self-revision outputs: "can it replace the original?" and "which is better designed?" [V] (pp. 5–6, 15–16).
58	- Validation against human judgement: logistic regression on metric differences predicting Win/Lose, 50/50 split of the 100 annotated pages, 435 pairwise annotations, 79.9% test accuracy; coefficients Block-Match 0.7429, Position 0.7605, CLIP 0.4929, Color 0.3461 (all p ≤ 0.001), Text −0.3541 (p = 0.021) [V] (p. 7). Simulated win rates from a refit linear model (text removed) correlate with human "win + tie" rates across 10 systems: Pearson r = 0.975, Kendall τ = 0.931 [V] (p. 17). Inter-annotator agreement: Fleiss' κ = 0.46 (pairwise), 0.32 (replaceability), 0.26 (which is better) [V] (p. 16).
59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): only regression coefficient p-values and correlation significance (Table 7, p < 0.05 marks) [V] (pp. 7, 15). No significance tests, confidence intervals or variance across runs for model comparisons — not reported.
60	
61	## 7. Key findings
62	1. GPT-4o is best on every automatic dimension (Direct: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4) [V] (p. 6); in human pairwise evaluation GPT-4o Direct wins 92% vs the Gemini baseline [V] (p. 7).
63	2. [A] Text-augmented prompting "increases the block-match score and text similarity score on most tested models" (p. 5). [V] Block-Match rises for 4 of 7 prompted models (e.g. GPT-4V 85.8 → 87.6; Gemini 80.2 → 84.8) but falls for GPT-4o (93.0 → 92.4), Claude 3 Opus (90.2 → 89.8) and Idefics2 (46.7 → 23.6); Text rises for all except Idefics2 (80.3 → 55.6) (Table 1, p. 6). [V] Self-revision helps GPT-4V and Claude 3 a little and does not help Gemini or open models (DeepSeek-VL self-revision collapses to Block 30.1) [V] (pp. 5–6).
64	3. Main weakness: models "mostly lag in recalling visual elements ... and generating correct layout designs" [A] (p. 1); on Design2Code-HARD, the authors state that state-of-the-art models "fail to generate 30% - 40% of the block elements" [A] (p. 8). Block-Match is an area-weighted share that also penalises hallucinated blocks (pp. 4–5), so it is not a count of missed elements [I]. [V] HARD Block-Match ranges 56.6–75.1 across configurations (GPT-4o Direct 56.6, i.e. more than 40% unmatched area) (Table 3, p. 8).
65	4. [A] Authors state that WebSight VLM-8B and Design2Code-18B "match Gemini direct prompting" (p. 6). [V] Design2Code-18B is close on Block (78.5 vs 80.2), but WebSight VLM-8B is far lower on Block (55.9) and Text (86.6 vs 94.6), though higher on CLIP (87.6 vs 84.4), Position (77.3 vs 72.3) and Color (79.4 vs 66.2) (Table 1, p. 6).
66	5. Direct assessment: 49% of GPT-4V self-revision pages judged interchangeable with the reference; generated pages preferred over the original in 64% of cases [V] (p. 6). Kappa for these questions is low (0.32, 0.26) [V] (p. 16).
67	6. Humans weight high-level layout and presence of content, not exact text: text similarity has a negative coefficient in predicting preference [V] (p. 7). Human and automatic rankings disagree in places (e.g. humans prefer WebSight VLM-8B over Design2Code-18B despite worse Block-Match/Text) [V] (pp. 6–7).
68	7. Total tag count is the strongest difficulty indicator (r = −0.28 with Block-Match for GPT-4V self-revision); non-English pages are harder [V] (pp. 8, 15).
69	8. Code quality, maintainability or functional behaviour of the generated code is not measured; all metrics are visual/textual on rendered screenshots [V] (pp. 3–4).
70	
71	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
72	- Better prompting is needed for complex pages, e.g. incremental generation of page parts [A] (p. 10).
73	- Training directly on real webpages is hard because they are long and noisy [A] (p. 10).
74	- Input is screenshot-only; Figma frames or sketches would need a re-designed evaluation [A] (p. 10).
75	- Only static webpages; dynamic pages need evaluation of "interactive functions beyond just visual similarity" [A] (p. 10).
76	- Human evaluation should not be "blindly trusted as the oracle" because of human top-down attention bias [A] (pp. 7–8).
77	- Text-block matching may be imperfect when granularity differs (non-contiguous merges not searched) [A] (p. 13).
78	
79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] Fidelity is purely visual (screenshot similarity). No functional, behavioural, or code-level quality measure (e.g. HTML validity, semantic structure, maintainability, responsiveness) — based on metric definitions pp. 3–4. For our project this means Design2Code says nothing about whether a rebuilt page works or is maintainable.
81	- [I] JavaScript, iframes, SVG and external links are stripped and prompts say no JS is needed (pp. 13–14); the task is reconstruction of a static, de-functionalised snapshot, not of an application.
82	- [I] Human validation is modest: 100 pages, Fleiss' κ only 0.46/0.32/0.26 (p. 16), logistic regression accuracy 79.9% on a 50-page test half (p. 7). The very high Pearson r = 0.975 is computed over only 10 system-level points (p. 17) and compares predicted wins with human "win + tie" — an aggregation that inflates agreement.
83	- [I] Test pages come from C4, a common pretraining corpus; data contamination is not discussed (grep for "contamin" finds nothing).
84	- [I] Single run per configuration with greedy decoding; no variance or significance testing between models (pp. 5–6, 14).
85	- [I] Design2Code-HARD pages are sourced from GitHub (p. 14) and filtered "using the same filtering process" (p. 8); how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described, so the HARD set's representativeness cannot be judged.
86	- [I] The metric-validation agreement is not out-of-sample. The logistic regression is trained on 50 of the 100 human-annotated pages (p. 7); the linear model for simulated win rates is refit "on the same training examples" and applied to "all 484 examples", which include those training pages (p. 17); and the human "win + tie" rates it is compared with come from the same 100 pages (Table 8, p. 17). So r = 0.975 / τ = 0.931 partly reflects fit on the training data, on top of being computed over only 10 system-level points.
87	- [I] Element metrics are text-anchored (blocks come from text segments, p. 13); images, icons and non-text elements are only covered by CLIP.
88	
89	## 10. Threats to validity
90	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): manual curation by the authors (selection bias towards well-formatted pages) (p. 13); possible C4 pretraining contamination (not discussed); Design2Code-18B checkpoint chosen on a 20-example dev set (p. 15) [I].
91	- External (generalisability of sample/context): static, single-page, English-dominant web pages with placeholders for media; HARD set of 80 (p. 8); no mobile apps, multi-page or interactive apps [I].
92	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): metrics measure visual similarity of a rendered screenshot, not functional fidelity or code quality; Text metric is negatively associated with human preference (p. 7), so the five metrics do not all point the same way [I].
93	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no CIs or tests for model differences; low-moderate inter-annotator agreement (p. 16); system-level correlation on n = 10 (p. 17), and that correlation is not an out-of-sample validation because the simulating model was fit on 50 of the same 100 annotated pages and applied to all 484 pages including them (pp. 7, 17) [I].
94	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): prompts, model versions and decoding settings reported (p. 14); fine-tuning hyper-parameters reported (p. 15); dataset release claimed but no link in our PDF (p. 10); commercial model versions may be deprecated [I].
95	
96	## 11. Future research directions
97	- Stated by authors [A]: incremental generation for complex pages; cleaning pipelines for training on real webpages; Figma/sketch inputs; dynamic webpages with interactive-function evaluation (p. 10); "generate UIs that support dynamic user interactions" (p. 9); website-design improvement tools (p. 6).
98	- Suggested by us [I]: pair the visual metrics with behavioural tests and static code-quality analysis of the generated HTML/CSS; report run-to-run variance; check pretraining contamination of C4-sourced pages.
99	
100	## 12. Relevance to our research
101	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
102	- How it informs our work [I]: Design2Code is the reference benchmark for screenshot-to-code reconstruction and the origin of the Block/Text/Position/Color/CLIP metric family reused by later work. It shows how visual fidelity can be measured and partly validated against humans, and it clearly leaves out interaction, functionality and code quality — the dimensions our project needs.
103	
104	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
105	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
106	|---|---|---|---|---|
107	| RQ1 | Screenshot-to-HTML/CSS with MLLMs via direct, text-augmented and self-revision prompting, plus fine-tuned open models | p. 4–5 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ2 | Visual fidelity measured by Block-Match, Text, Position, Color (CIEDE2000) and CLIP on rendered screenshots | p. 3–5 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | GPT-4o Direct best: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4 on 484 pages | p. 6 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ2 | Authors state SOTA models fail to generate 30–40% of block elements on 80 HARD pages | p. 8 | A | weak |
111	| RQ2 | HARD Block-Match (area-weighted, also penalises hallucinated blocks) ranges 56.6–75.1 across configurations (GPT-4o Direct 56.6) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
112	| RQ2 | 49% of GPT-4V self-revision pages judged interchangeable with the original (κ = 0.32) | p. 6, 16 | V | weak |
113	| RQ3 | No code quality or maintainability measure; only rendered visual similarity | p. 3–4 | V | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | Metrics predict human Win/Lose with 79.9% accuracy (logistic regression, 50-page test half); Text coefficient negative | p. 7 | V | moderate |
115	| RQ4 | Simulated vs human win rates: Pearson r = 0.975, Kendall τ = 0.931 over 10 systems; not out-of-sample (model fit on 50 of the same 100 annotated pages, applied to all 484 incl. them) | p. 7, 17 | V | weak |
116	| RQ4 | Human agreement low-moderate: Fleiss' κ 0.46 / 0.32 / 0.26 | p. 16 | V | moderate |
117	| RQ4 | No significance tests or variance across runs for model comparisons | p. 5–6 | I | moderate |
118	| RQ5 | Authors call for dynamic webpages evaluated on interactive functions beyond visual similarity | p. 10 | A | moderate |
119	
120	## 14. Key quotes
121	> "models mostly lag in recalling visual elements from the input webpages and generating correct layout designs" (p. 1)
122	> "We find that 49% of the AI-generated webpages are considered exchangeable with the reference webpages." (p. 6)
123	> "This also requires the evaluation to consider interactive functions beyond just visual similarity." (p. 10)
124

126	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–19), including appendices A–I; reference list skimmed only.
127	- Source version: ACL Anthology PDF of the NAACL 2025 long paper (ACL proceedings page numbers printed in the footer, e.g. 3960 on PDF p. 5), not the arXiv preprint; all page refs follow this PDF.
128	- Uncertainties: dataset/code URL not given in our ACL PDF (the arXiv version may differ); how HARD pages were found on GitHub (pp. 8, 14); the logistic-regression test-set size in pairs is not stated separately (435 is the total of usable pairs). Peer-reviewed (NAACL 2025, tier 1).

18	# Interaction2Code: Benchmarking MLLM-based Interactive Webpage Code Generation from Interactive Prototyping
19	
20	- Authors: Xiao, Jingyu; Wan, Yuxuan; Huo, Yintong; Wang, Zixin; Xu, Xinyi; Wang, Wenxuan; Xu, Zhiyao; Wang, Yuhang; Lyu, Michael R.
21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/ase63991.2025.00028
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index), extracted from arXiv:2411.03292v3 (1 Mar 2026), not the ASE proceedings PDF
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Formulate the Interaction-to-Code task (generate an interactive webpage from an "interactive prototype": screenshots before and after each interaction), build a real-world benchmark for it, and systematically study how well MLLMs reproduce webpage interactions, why they fail, and how prompting can help [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- No formal RQs. The study is organised around four reported "limitations" of MLLMs: (1) worse generation of interactive parts than of the full page; (2) ten failure types; (3) poor performance on visually subtle interactions; (4) insufficient understanding from visual input alone — each paired with an improvement strategy [V] (pp. 1–2).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction plus empirical comparison of models and prompts; automatic evaluation via Selenium-driven interaction replay; human usability and pairwise evaluation; qualitative failure taxonomy; sub-experiments on visual saliency and input modality; ablation; small user study [V] (pp. 3–11).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: MLLM receives the original screenshot plus post-interaction screenshot(s) and must output one HTML+CSS+JavaScript file, tagging interactive elements with ids (e.g. id="interact1") so a webdriver can trigger them [V] (pp. 3–5). Prompts: Direct, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Mark (red bounding boxes on interactive areas), Failure-aware Prompt (FAP: lists the ten failure types) [V] (p. 5). Further enhancements: Visual Saliency Enhancement (crop to enlarge the interaction area) and adding human-written textual descriptions of interactions [V] (pp. 9–10).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o-20240806, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620, Qwen2.5-VL-instruct 3B/7B/72B; Direct prompting is the baseline for prompt comparisons; Gemini-1.5-flash Direct is the human pairwise baseline [V] (pp. 4, 6). No non-LLM or prior UI-to-code system (e.g. DCGen) is run as a baseline [I] (based on p. 4 model list).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): (1) C4 validation set (CommonCrawl), filtered as in Design2Code, 1,000 pages sampled across 15 topics, from which four PhD students each picked about 25 → 100 pages; (2) 27 popular GitHub projects (average 13k stars) with deployed links, found via "open-production-web-projects" and "awesome-opensource-apps", to include UI-framework pages [V] (pp. 2–3).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 127 webpages and 374 interactions; 15+ topics; 23 tag categories and 8 visual categories (31 interaction categories) [V] (pp. 1, 3). Most frequent interactive tags: button 235, input 52, span 37, link 36 [V] (p. 3).
42	- Sampling / selection method: manual selection by four PhD students for complexity (at least one meaningful interaction) and diversity; 1–10 "important and functional" interactions kept per page; trivial interactions (e.g. hover underline) excluded [V] (pp. 2–3). Selection guidelines are only in the external artifact [V] (p. 3).
43	- Data availability (public? link?): data and code at https://github.com/WebPAI/Interaction2Code [A] (p. 1).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: temperature 0; max output 4,096 tokens (commercial) and 2,048 (Qwen); other parameters default [V] (p. 4). Selenium webdriver locates elements by id, performs the interaction and screenshots the result; the changed region is extracted by pixel subtraction (same-size pages) or a Git-diff of rows/columns (size-changing pages) (Algorithm 1) [V] (p. 4). Data-contamination check: BLEU between generated and original HTML is 0.12–0.14 for the four main models [V] (p. 5). FAP experiment: 2/3 of the dataset used to derive failure types, 1/3 for testing [V] (p. 8). Saliency and modality experiments use 10 randomly sampled failure-case webpages each [V] (pp. 9–10).
47	- Code availability: GitHub repository above [A] (p. 1). Appendix H (tool) and detailed human-evaluation instructions are referenced but are not in our 13-page PDF [V] (pp. 6, 11).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Full-page metrics: CLIP score (visual similarity); SSIM (structural similarity); Text similarity = BLEU on OCR-extracted text; Widget Similarity (WS) and Widget Match Rate (WMR) computed with the GUIPilot method [V] (p. 4).
51	- Interaction-part metrics (on the extracted changed region): CLIP, SSIM, Text; Position similarity P = 1 − max(|xo − xg|, |yo − yg|) of normalised interaction-area centres; Implement Rate IR = implemented / (implemented + unimplemented), where "implemented" means detectable by the webdriver [V] (p. 4).
52	- Human metrics: Usability Rate UR = usable / (usable + unusable), judged by four PhD students (three years front-end experience) — usable if the implementation "precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype"; pairwise Win/Tie/Lose by five annotators against Gemini-1.5-flash Direct, majority (≥3) rule; failure-type annotation [V] (pp. 4, 6–7).
53	- Validation against human judgement: authors state human results "are consistent with Section V-A, confirming the validity of our automatic evaluation metrics" [A] (p. 6). No correlation coefficient, agreement statistic or regression is reported — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement for usability, pairwise or failure annotation — not reported (failure types reached by discussion to consensus on a 25% sample) [V] (p. 7). Number of items in the human evaluations — not reported.
54	- Widget metrics are acknowledged as unreliable for web pages: WS is "consistently poor" (0.02–0.05) and GUIPilot omits many elements because it was designed for mobile UIs [V] (pp. 5–6).
55	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none for model or prompt comparisons; saliency effect described as "significantly increases" without a test [V] (pp. 8–9). Not reported.
56	
57	## 7. Key findings
58	1. Interactive parts are generated worse than full pages for all models (e.g. GPT-4o average full-page CLIP 0.7059 vs interaction-part CLIP 0.5598) [V] (p. 6).
59	2. Claude-3.5-Sonnet has the best averages on most metrics (e.g. interaction IR 0.7870, full-page Text 0.5835); GPT-4o with Mark prompt has the highest single IR (0.8128); Qwen2.5-VL-72B ≈ Gemini-1.5-flash; performance rises with model size [V] (pp. 5–6).
60	3. Human Usability Rate (Fig. 6a, read from figure labels): GPT-4o Direct/CoT/Mark 73/74/81%; Claude 66/69/77%; Gemini 47/53/64%; Qwen-72B 41/43/54%; Qwen-3B 17–19% [V] (p. 6). Mark prompting gives the largest usability gain (Claude +11 points vs Direct) [V] (p. 6).
61	4. Ten failure types in two groups (interactive element: missing, no interaction, wrong element, wrong type, wrong position; interaction effects: wrong position, wrong type, effect on wrong element, partial implementation, wrong function) [V] (pp. 7–8). Failures (a) missing element, (b) no interaction and (j) wrong function have usability <10% (0%, 6.93%, 0%) [V] (pp. 7–8). Main failure modes are "No interaction", "Partial implementation", "Interactive element missing" and "Wrong function" [A] (p. 8).
62	5. Failures cluster into spatial (a, c, e, f), type (d, g) and behavioural (b, h, i, j) failures [A] (p. 8).
63	6. Low visual saliency (small interaction area) lowers SSIM and position similarity; cropping to enlarge the area (1.2–3×) recovers interactions on 10 failure pages [V] (pp. 9–10).
64	7. Authors state that combined visual + text input "consistently outperforms single-modality inputs across all prompt types" [A] (p. 10). On 10 failure pages with GPT-4o, V+T is best on most cells (e.g. Direct: Position 0.7157 V+T vs 0.3951 V) [V] (p. 10), but not all: under the Mark prompt, SSIM for V+T is 0.4336, below V (0.4520) and T (0.4454) [V] (p. 10). All four enhancements combined give the best ablation result (GPT-4o interaction CLIP 0.6937 vs 0.5700) [V] (p. 11).
65	8. FAP: authors claim it improves "all models" [A] (p. 8), but Table VI shows Qwen2.5-VL-3B drops on 7 of 8 metrics and Qwen-7B on 5 of 8 [V] (p. 9).
66	9. User study: with the tool, 4 tasks took 279 s vs 413 s on average and expert similarity rating 4.5 vs 3.875 (two participants per condition, two raters) [V] (p. 11).
67	10. Code quality or maintainability of the generated HTML/CSS/JS is not measured; the only code-level measure is BLEU against the original HTML, used as a contamination check [V] (pp. 4–5).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- Limited context length: complex pages with many interactions may exceed the context window; iterative generation suggested [A] (p. 11).
71	- Model selection: only three main commercial MLLMs tested; others (e.g. Pixtral) left for future work [A] (p. 11).
72	- Back-end interactions (login, search) cannot be evaluated because the benchmark has no back-end code [A] (p. 11).
73	- Existing widget-consistency methods are designed for mobile UIs and miss web elements [A] (p. 5).
74	
75	## 9. Limitations we identified
76	- [I] Validation of automatic metrics against humans is only a qualitative "consistent" statement (p. 6); no correlation, agreement (kappa) or item counts are given. The automatic metrics are therefore not shown to measure functional fidelity.
77	- [I] "Implement Rate" counts an interaction as implemented if the webdriver can find and trigger the element (p. 4) — this measures presence, not correct behaviour; functional correctness rests on the human Usability Rate alone.
78	- [I] Interaction fidelity is judged on screenshots of state changes, not on behavioural traces or DOM/state assertions; non-visual effects (data, network, storage) are out of scope (based on pp. 3–4, 11).
79	- [I] Several sub-experiments use only 10 pages (pp. 9–10) and the user study has 2 participants per condition (p. 11); these results are anecdotal.
80	- [I] The FAP claim ("improve ... on all models", p. 8) contradicts the paper's own Table VI (p. 9) for the two smaller Qwen models.
81	- [I] Similarly, the modality claim that V+T "consistently outperforms" single modalities "across all prompt types" (p. 10) is contradicted by Table VIII for SSIM under the Mark prompt (V+T 0.4336 < V 0.4520 and T 0.4454, p. 10), and rests on only 10 pages.
82	- [I] The FAP test uses failure types derived from 2/3 of the same dataset (p. 8); split procedure and whether it is by page or by interaction is not stated.
83	- [I] Fig. 9 "No failure" shares (about 36% for GPT-4o, about 40% for Claude, read from the figure, p. 9) look hard to reconcile with Usability Rates of 73–81% (p. 6); the denominators/definitions are not explained.
84	- [I] The contamination argument (C4 has only text; BLEU 0.12–0.14, p. 5) is weak: C4 URLs' HTML is widely crawled elsewhere, and low BLEU does not rule out memorised layout.
85	- [I] No code-quality, maintainability or code-structure measurement, despite generating JavaScript event logic.
86	
87	## 10. Threats to validity
88	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): pages and interactions hand-picked by the authors' annotators (pp. 2–3); FAP failure types derived from the same benchmark (p. 8); Table VI direct baselines differ from Table IV (different subset), so improvements are relative to a subset [I].
89	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 127 pages, front-end only, no back-end; mostly click-type interactions on buttons (235 of tagged elements) (p. 3); single-file output, not multi-file framework projects [I].
90	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): visual metrics on changed regions approximate interaction fidelity; IR measures element presence; widget metrics admitted unreliable for web (p. 5) [I].
91	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single deterministic run (temperature 0); no tests, CIs or agreement statistics; small N in sub-studies [I].
92	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and code released (p. 1); prompts shown (p. 5); key guidelines and appendix only in the artifact; the PDF is arXiv v3 (1 Mar 2026), the ASE 2025 version may differ [I].
93	
94	## 11. Future research directions
95	- Stated by authors [A]: iterative multi-round generation for many interactions; testing more MLLMs (e.g. Pixtral) (p. 11); handling interactions that require back-end code (p. 11); designing widget-level consistency detection suited to web pages (pp. 5–6).
96	- Suggested by us [I]: validate interaction metrics against human usability with reported correlations; add behavioural assertions (DOM state, event sequences) and code-quality/maintainability analysis of generated JS; extend to multi-page apps with back-end.
97	
98	## 12. Relevance to our research
99	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence).
100	- How it informs our work [I]: this is the closest web benchmark to reverse engineering from observable behaviour: input is before/after screenshots of interactions, and the target is a page that reproduces that behaviour. It supplies a usable failure taxonomy and the Usability Rate as a human functional-fidelity measure, but its automatic metrics are weakly validated and it ignores code quality.
101	
102	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
103	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
104	|---|---|---|---|---|
105	| RQ1 | Interaction-to-Code: MLLM generates one HTML/CSS/JS file from before/after interaction screenshots; Direct, CoT, Mark, FAP prompts | p. 2–5 | V | moderate |
106	| RQ2 | Interaction fidelity measured by interaction-part CLIP/SSIM/Text/Position, Implement Rate (webdriver), and human Usability Rate | p. 4 | V | moderate |
107	| RQ2 | Best human Usability Rate 81% (GPT-4o Mark); Claude 66–77%; Qwen-3B 17–19% (number of evaluated items not reported, p. 6) | p. 6 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ2 | Interactive parts scored lower than full pages for all six models | p. 6 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | Ten failure types; missing element, no interaction, wrong function yield <10% usability | p. 7–8 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ3 | No code quality or maintainability measured; code compared to original only via BLEU 0.12–0.14 for contamination | p. 5 | V | moderate |
111	| RQ4 | Automatic metrics declared "consistent" with human evaluation; no correlation or inter-annotator agreement reported | p. 6 | V | weak |
112	| RQ4 | Widget Similarity/Match (GUIPilot) unreliable for web pages (WS 0.02–0.05) | p. 5–6 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | Claimed FAP gain on all models contradicted by Table VI for Qwen-3B/7B | p. 8–9 | V | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | Saliency, modality sub-studies on 10 pages; user study 2 vs 2 participants | p. 9–11 | V | weak |
115	| RQ5 | Back-end-dependent interactions (login, search) not evaluable; future work | p. 11 | A | moderate |
116	
117	## 14. Key quotes
118	> "existing benchmarks only contain static web pages for evaluation and ignore the dynamic interaction" (p. 1)
119	> "An interaction is considered usable if its implementation precisely matches the behavior specified in the interactive prototype." (p. 6)
120	> "The benchmark we collect does not include back-end code; we cannot verify the generation effect of such interactions" (p. 11)
121	
122	## Analyst notes
123	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–13); garbled Figure 6 and Table VI/Figure 9 checked on PDF pages 6, 8 and 9. References skimmed. Appendix H and annotation guidelines are external (artifact) and were not read.
124	- Uncertainties: usability percentages are read from figure labels (p. 6); Fig. 9 percentages are approximate. Our PDF is arXiv v3 (dated 1 Mar 2026), later than the ASE 2025 publication; page numbers refer to this PDF. Peer-reviewed (ASE 2025, tier 1). Same group (CUHK, Lyu) as DesignBench/DCGen — related benchmarks in our set may share authors and methods.
125

220	## Contradictions
221	<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->
222	
223	Each entry records both sides with page refs, then compares data, population, method, metric and time. Explanations are labelled [I]. We do not pick a side.
224	
225	### C1. Does AI assistance harm maintainability? he2026speed vs borg2026echoes
226	- **Side A** [V]: Cursor adoption in 806 OSS repositories raised total SonarQube static-analysis warnings by +30.26% and total cognitive complexity by +41.64% relative to matched controls (Borusyak DiD) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The complexity effect stays significant after controlling for codebase size in the GMM (0.086, p<0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
227	- **Side B** [V]: When a second developer evolved AI-co-developed code without AI, there was no significant difference in completion time [@borg2026echoes, p. 33], CodeHealth (8.49 vs 8.44) [@borg2026echoes, p. 38] or test coverage [@borg2026echoes, p. 35]. The only "significant" maintainability effect, a Bayesian +0.10 CodeHealth for code from habitual AI users, favours AI [@borg2026echoes, p. 39].
228	- **Differences**:
229	  - Data and population: real-world OSS repositories with ≥10 stars [@he2026speed, p. 4] vs one 2 KLoC Java/Spring Boot task done by 151 volunteer professionals [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @borg2026echoes, p. 64].
230	  - Tool generation: an agentic IDE (Cursor Composer/agent) [@he2026speed, p. 2] vs late-2024 assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) [@borg2026echoes, p. 3; @borg2026echoes, p. 60].
231	  - Metric: repository-total warnings and cognitive complexity, which scale with code size [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a LoC-weighted file-level CodeHealth average plus a second developer's evolution time [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
232	  - Time: monthly panel of up to about 20 months [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a single hand-off task.
233	  - Robustness: he2026speed's quality effects turn negative and non-significant under the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%) [@he2026speed, p. 16]. borg2026echoes is underpowered (75 of 128 planned participants; 80% power only for d≈0.66) [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
234	- **Partial agreement** [V]: borg2026echoes' observational Phase 1 also found more duplication (23% vs 11%), more complex conditionals and very large code-volume outliers in AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 30; @borg2026echoes, p. 46]. With size controlled, he2026speed finds no direct Cursor effect on warnings [@he2026speed, p. 8].
235	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two results need not conflict. Both fit "AI adds more code, and project-level totals rise with it, while per-file health and the short-term effort of the next developer are not clearly worse". The he2026speed effect depends on the estimator, and borg2026echoes can rule out only large effects. Neither study settles the question.
236	
237	### C2. Fewer or more static-analysis issues in LLM code? molison2025llm vs he2026speed
238	- **Side A** [V]: GPT-4o solutions had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged "bugs" than APPS human solutions (OR 0.00–0.019) [@molison2025llm, p. 8], and lower SonarQube fix effort on introductory and interview tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 7].
239	- **Side B** [V]: Cursor adoption raised repository SonarQube warnings by +30.26% [@he2026speed, p. 7].
240	- **Differences**:
241	  - Unit: per-solution odds of an issue in single-file stdin/stdout programs [@molison2025llm, p. 5] vs monthly repository totals [@he2026speed, p. 5].
242	  - Baseline: competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability [@molison2025llm, p. 9] vs matched non-adopting repositories, which may themselves use other AI tools [@he2026speed, p. 7].
243	  - Metric: the SonarQube "bug" category vs all reliability, maintainability and security warnings.
244	  - Leakage: molison2025llm's few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
245	  - Time: GPT-4o in 2024 vs Cursor agents in 2024–2025.
246	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the results are not comparable. Both use SonarQube, but the units, baselines and code types differ, so neither one refutes the other. molison2025llm's smell results are themselves mixed: zero-shot code had 3.57x the odds of a smell on introductory tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
247	
248	### C3. Which instrument measures the quality of AI code? zhu2026understanding vs SonarQube-based studies
249	- **Side A** [A]: zhu2026understanding chose PyExamine to separate structural and architectural smells from the "superficial linting issues" counted by SonarQube [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2; @zhu2026understanding, p. 4]. It found more Long Method smells in larger LLMs' code than in human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
250	- **Side B** [V]: SonarQube-based studies report fewer issues in LLM code [@molison2025llm, p. 8], a platform-dependent issue density (22.83 vs about 9 issues/KLOC) [@mota2026comparing, p. 5], or more warnings with adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7].
251	- **Context** [A]: technical-debt tools disagree on what counts as real debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5], and SonarQube and general linters were not designed for LLM-specific debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22]. mota2026comparing calls SonarQube an auxiliary indicator only [@mota2026comparing, p. 6]. borg2026echoes argues that CodeHealth outperforms the SonarQube Maintainability Rating; note that its first author works for CodeScene, the vendor of CodeHealth [@borg2026echoes, p. 4; @borg2026echoes, p. 75].
252	- **Differences**: the tools differ (PyExamine, SonarQube, CodeHealth, MI), and so do the task types (algorithmic snippets, generated web apps, OSS repositories). zhu2026understanding's Exp I counts are small, unnormalised and untested [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
253	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the direction of "LLM vs human code quality" may depend on the measuring instrument. The field has no validated, size-normalised maintainability measure for AI-generated code.
254	
255	### C4. Does iterative feedback or self-repair help? pan2026functional vs tran2026vibe / zhou2025declarui / wu2026looks
256	- **Side A** [V]: On GPT-5.2, three one-shot strategies all lowered the aggregate non-functional score without raising functional correctness: self-repair, environment repair and planning (NF 46.1–49.9% vs 57.1% at baseline) [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
257	- **Side B**:
258	  - [V] Browser self-testing during generation correlates with accuracy across 16 models (r = 0.72) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
259	  - [V] Removing DeclarUI's page-transition graph plus refinement loop cuts navigation coverage to 23.1% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10]. Its compile success is 98% vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9].
260	  - [V]/[A] A tsc + vite verify-repair loop gives 100% build success for all six models [@wu2026looks, p. 6]. The authors attribute this to the loop [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
261	- **Further evidence** [A]: agents' own validation missed behavioural mismatches with the reference [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
262	- **Differences**:
263	  - Feedback type: generic one-shot repair of a whole Python repository [@pan2026functional, p. 8], targeted compile and navigation checks [@zhou2025declarui, p. 5], and build checks [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
264	  - Design: a single-model intervention (pan2026functional) vs an observational correlation across models, where the system prompt itself demands browser testing [@tran2026vibe, p. 16].
265	  - Outcome: non-functional quality (pan2026functional) vs compilation, navigation or build (zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks).
266	  - Circularity: zhou2025declarui scores navigation against the same graph that guides its refinement [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
267	- **Possible explanation** [I]: feedback improves the property it checks (compilation, build, navigation edges). Self-testing goes along with stronger models. No study shows that generic repair improves both behavioural fidelity and code quality, and the only study that measures quality after repair finds harm (single model, single run).
268	
269	### C5. Do rebuilds "look right but behave wrong"? chen2025iwr / lu2025webgen / xiao2025benchmarking vs bai2026recreationworld / wu2026looks
270	- **Side A** [V]:
271	  - Interactive functionality is below visual fidelity for all 28 models (GPT-5 IFS 24.39 vs VFS 64.25) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
272	  - Design-validation tests are passed more often than functional tests (e.g. 44.3% vs 21.1%) [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
273	  - Interactive regions score lower than full pages for all six models [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
274	- **Side B** [V]:
275	  - In bai2026recreationworld the visual (VLM) channel is below the programmatic channel for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11], although static structure beats actions within the programmatic tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
276	  - In wu2026looks navigation passes 58–92% [@wu2026looks, p. 7], while visual fidelity stays at or below 2.99/5 [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
277	- **Differences**:
278	  - chen2025iwr's VFS is averaged only over reached checkpoints, so part of its IFS<VFS gap comes from how the metrics are built [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
279	  - Visual scores come from different instruments: OCR+DINO+MLLM rubric, VLM assertions, Borda ranks and CLIP.
280	  - Functional scores also differ: action replay, accessibility tests and navigation tests.
281	- **Possible explanation** [I]: bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr are only *directionally consistent* on one point: static structure is reproduced more easily than interaction logic. The broader claim "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity" is not supported, because the visual and functional scales are not commensurable across or within papers.
282	
283	### C6. Multi-agent / agentic frameworks: MetaGPT fails in liu2026benchmarking but leads in mock2026vibe
284	- **Side A** [V]: MetaGPT nearly always fails on E2EDev (0–5.4% Req.Acc) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6]. Multi-agent frameworks "do not consistently improve" over a plain LLM (by our count, 9 of 24 cells higher [I]) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
285	- **Side B** [V]: Agentic MetaGPT X runs had the highest test pass rate (mean 94.58%) [@mock2026vibe, p. 25; @mock2026vibe, p. 41]. zhu2026understanding generated complete multi-file apps with MetaGPT, but only after adding explicit modularity prompts [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
286	- **Differences**:
287	  - Task size: a two-function string task [@mock2026vibe, p. 12] vs 46 multi-requirement web apps.
288	  - Backbone: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] vs older or smaller backbones such as GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
289	  - Product: MetaGPT X web interface vs the open-source framework.
290	  - Evaluation: 12 runs pooled vs 46 projects x 3 runs.
291	- **Possible explanation** [I]: framework value depends on the backbone and the task scale. mock2026vibe's agentic advantage is confounded with the newer model generation.
292	
293	### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe
294	- **Side A** [V]: Reference-normalised security averages 87.40% and is the strongest non-functional dimension [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
295	- **Side B** [V]: 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best agent fail targeted security tests, and SecPass is only 3.8–12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
296	- **Differences**: pan2026functional counts high-risk static findings relative to the reference, and the score can reward incomplete code. zhao2025vibe runs 3.5 targeted security tests per task for a known historical CWE [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. The tasks also differ: whole-repository generation vs security-sensitive feature patches.
297	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two instruments measure different things, a static absence of flagged patterns vs exploit-relevant behaviour. "Secure" cannot be compared across them.
298	
299	### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
300	- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. In bai2026recreationworld they are 89.4% smaller with 92.3% fewer files (4 of 10 models; desktop and Android only) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. In yang2026programbench they are shorter (median 1,173 vs 3,068 lines) and use fewer files [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
301	- **Side B** [V]:
302	  - Cursor adoption raises lines added by +281.3% in month 1 [@he2026speed, p. 8].
303	  - AI-assisted Task 1 code produced outliers of up to 10,788 lines [@borg2026echoes, p. 30].
304	  - In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts track code size (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
305	  - The visual-fidelity leader writes 1,441 LoC vs 668 for GPT-5 [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
306	- **Differences**: rebuilds from scratch scored against a behavioural oracle of a mature original, vs incremental additions to existing projects or apps generated from a spec.
307	- **Possible explanation** [I]: reconstructions under-implement the original, which is consistent with low full-pass rates. Assisted development adds volume. Size therefore carries opposite signals in the two settings, and size-driven quality metrics (smell counts, totals) must be normalised before comparison.
308	
309	### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)
310	- **"Vibe coding" means different things** [V]:
311	  - fawzy2026vibe: natural-language prompting plus re-prompting with minimal review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
312	  - asdaque2026novice: a supervised agent workflow, operationalised as opening agentic PRs [@asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. Its authors warn that the findings may not hold under a broader definition [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4].
313	  - mock2026vibe: human-written TDD tests plus scripted prompts that participants could not modify [@mock2026vibe, p. 15].
314	  - he2026speed: Cursor configuration files committed to a repository (intent-to-treat) [@he2026speed, p. 4].
315	  - ehsani2026faster: a driver of fast-integration debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 17].
316	  - [I] These are different interventions. Their results should not be pooled as "effects of vibe coding".
317	- **Fidelity scores are not comparable** [V]:
318	  - 58.06% average of programmatic and VLM channels [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
319	  - 36.35 Final Score (0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
320	  - 49.15% cumulative workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
321	  - 53.75% Req.Acc with `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
322	  - 27.8% UI-agent accuracy with half credit for PARTIAL [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
323	  - 61.77% workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 6].
324	  - 0% resolved / 3% almost [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
325	  - [I] Each figure uses a different oracle, input, application type and model generation. Do not rank across them.
326	
327	### C10. Same model family builds or judges the benchmark and is evaluated (possible bias; untested)
328	- **Overlap and the same family wins** [V]:
329	  - yang2026programbench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 wrote the tests [@yang2026programbench, p. 3], and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 31].
330	  - tran2026vibe: GPT-5 drafted the specs [@tran2026vibe, p. 3], and GPT-5.3-Codex ranks first [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]. The canonical judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5 [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
331	  - kim2026programdistill: GPT-5.6 Sol builds the tasks [@kim2026programdistill, p. 2], GPT-6 Astra ranks first [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8], and GPT-6 Astra also classifies the failures [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
332	  - zhao2025vibe: Claude 4 Sonnet runs the environment-building agent [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17], and SWE-agent constructs the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. The best setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
333	- **Overlap without a visible advantage** [V]:
334	  - liu2026benchmarking: GPT-4o built the annotations and is evaluated [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 13]; the best backbone is Claude-Haiku.
335	  - lu2025webgen: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and scored low [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
336	  - bai2026recreationworld: the Qwen3.7-Plus judge is the lowest-scoring model (average 9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
337	  - chen2025iwr: the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge ranks mid-table [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
338	  - wu2026looks: the judge is Gemini 2.5 Pro, Opus leads [@wu2026looks, p. 13], and the authors report no self-preference [A].
339	- [I] No paper tests construction-model or judge-model self-preference directly. The pattern is a validity threat, not a demonstrated bias.
340	
341	## Agreements / converging evidence
342	
343	- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
344	  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
345	  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
346	  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
347	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
348	- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
349	  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
350	  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
351	  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
352	  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
353	  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
354	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
355	- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
356	- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
357	  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
358	  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
359	  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
360	  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
361	  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
362	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
363	- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
364	- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
365	  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
366	  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
367	  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
368	  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
369	- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
370	  - Judge–human agreement ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the evaluator model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
371	  - 86–94% raw agreement on 3 settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
372	  - τ = 0.716 on 55 author-labelled scenarios [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
373	  - ρ = 0.65, tuned in-sample [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
374	  - Low human inter-annotator κ (0.26–0.46) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
375	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**.
376	- **G-A8. Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as fast but flawed** [V]: [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8]. This converges with LLM-linked code and design debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16] and with higher review burden for novice agent users [@asdaque2026novice, p. 3]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on perception and proxy evidence, not code measurement.
377

## RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
> **Takeaway:** When AI agents rebuild real apps by using a running original, even the best agent averages only 58.06% and passes every functional test on just 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11]. The rebuilds are also much smaller and more concentrated in a few files than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. This is the closest study to our topic, but it does not measure code quality.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Shuai Bai, Jiayong Deng, Sicheng Fan, Yikun Fu, Chang Gao, Xuhao Hu, et al. (33 authors, Alibaba Group) |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed); industry paper |
| Identifier | DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2609.22000 (arXiv 2609.22000) |
| Paper type | Benchmark and environment framework, with a model comparison and a training (transfer) experiment |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3 (partly), RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
Imagine giving an AI a working app, but not its source code, and asking it to build a copy that behaves the same way. That is "application recreation", and it is very close to what we call AI-assisted reverse engineering. The authors built a large test set for this task on five platforms: Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and the Web [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]. They tested ten of the newest AI models, studied how the agents worked, and looked at the code they produced. They also checked whether practising this task helps AI models on other coding tasks [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 3].

### How they did it
1. They collected 250 reference apps. Desktop and Android apps came from open-source projects. The Web set has 44 sites the authors made themselves and 6 real, openly licensed sites [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7].
2. Each agent got a task prompt, live access to the running original, and a computer with GUI control (the ability to look at and click an interface) and developer tools. It had to hand back source code that builds and launches [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]. On desktop and Android the agent could not see the original's source code. On the Web, the page code sent to the browser is necessarily visible [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]. Each attempt had up to 20 hours [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 4].
3. Hidden tests were written by AI agents, replayed on a clean copy of the original, cleaned of unstable cases, and reviewed by humans before being frozen [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].
4. Two scores were computed [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9]. The Programmatic score is the share of tests passed; the tests read text, buttons and values through the accessibility interface (the system layer that screen readers use). The VLM score uses a vision-language model (an AI that reads images) as a judge, which checks screenshots against statements about the original. An app that does not build scores zero.
5. They then analysed agent behaviour and code size for four of the models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12].

### Data and setup
- 250 tasks, 50 per platform [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7].
- Median original size: 49.3k lines of code on Ubuntu, 13.5k on macOS, 6.7k on Windows, 15.0k on Android [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].
- 10 models. GPT models ran in the Codex tool and all others in Claude Code [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28].
- Network access was blocked by default, and reference and test files were protected [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
- Runs per task are not reported. [I] Our reviewers think it was probably one run, because one single-run comparison reproduces a main-table score exactly [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- 35,000 recreation runs were used as training data for the transfer experiment [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 5].

### Key findings
- [V] GPT-6 Astra leads with an average of 58.06 (Programmatic 58.19, VLM 57.92). Next are Claude Opus 5 (44.16) and GPT-5.6 Sol (42.06); Qwen3.7-Plus is lowest (9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [V] Full fidelity is rare. The best model passes at least 90% of tests on 17.6% of apps and all tests on 2.8%; every other model reaches at most 5.53% and 0.8% [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [V] Agents copy what an interface contains better than what it does. Structure tests had the highest pass rate in 15 of 16 native comparisons, and the weakest category trailed by 9.1 to 34.4 points [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
- [V] Rebuilds are smaller: 89.4% have less code than the original (median 16.9% of its size), and 92.3% use fewer files [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15].
- [V] More code did not mean better fidelity. Among the four analysed models, Claude Opus 5 wrote the most code, while the top model GPT-6 Astra wrote the least on four of five platforms [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15].
- [V] Agents often switched to a different UI framework, for example rebuilding 75% of Electron, Tauri or Wails desktop apps natively. [A] The authors call this "architectural substitution rather than implementation quality" [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
- [V] Agents rarely checked their final work: the full "edit, relaunch, inspect" loop appears in only 23.6% to 47.5% of runs [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12].
- [V] Copying from the original seems rare: median exact-line overlap is 0.014% to 0.088% [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 18].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] A finite test suite "cannot establish equivalence across all states and interaction paths" [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- [A] Public originals may be in the models' training data [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- [A] The behaviour and code analyses are descriptive, so they do not show cause and effect [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 3].
- [A] Android isolation is weaker, and Web cannot hide the source [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 10].
- [I] No confidence intervals and probably one run per task, so small gaps between models may not be stable [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [I] All authors are from Alibaba, and Qwen models serve as judge and as training-data generator. No conflict-of-interest statement is given [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 5]. The Qwen judge model scored lowest, so no favourable self-scoring is visible [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [I] Model and tool are mixed up: GPT ran in Codex, the rest in Claude Code [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28].
- [I] One Web site that replayed copied content escaped the cheating detector and kept a 54.82% Programmatic score [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 47].
- [I] Code size and file counts are not quality measures [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- G1: code is described only by size and structure, never by maintainability [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15].
- G2: the VLM judge is never checked against human ratings, and self-preference is not tested [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
- G4: agents' weak self-checking [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12] raises the question of whether better feedback loops would help.
- G5: the authors suggest newly built originals to reduce training-data risk [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- G6: [I] there is no human-developer or human-steered condition.
- G8: it is the only project paper with native Android rebuilds [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7], but apps needing login or remote services were excluded [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].

### Why it matters for your research
[I] This is the strongest benchmark evidence that rebuilding apps from observation is possible but far from complete. You can reuse its design ideas: tests checked against the original, two scoring channels, a coverage audit and network isolation. Its main gap is your opportunity: it shows that rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic, but not whether they are harder to maintain. Do not copy its weak points: report several runs, validate any AI judge against humans, and keep model and tool separate.

### Connections to other papers
- Agrees with yang2026programbench: rebuilds are shorter and use fewer files than the originals [@yang2026programbench, p. 9], and full equivalence is rare there too (0 of 200 programs) [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
- Builds on ProgramBench: it is one of the benchmarks used to test training transfer [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 6].
- Agrees with kim2026programdistill: agents rebuilding web apps from a live original recover only 49.15% of workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11], and their self-checks miss errors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
- Only partly agrees with chen2025iwr. Both find interaction harder than static structure [@chen2025iwr, p. 16]. But here the visual score is below the programmatic score for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11], so "looks right but behaves wrong" is not supported in general.
- Places Design2Code and Interaction2Code as earlier, narrower web benchmarks [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 21].

It had to hand back source code that builds and launches [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]. On desktop and Android the agent could not see the original's source code. On the Web, the page code sent to the browser is necessarily visible [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]. Each attempt had up to 20 hours [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 4].
3. Hidden tests were written by AI agents, replayed on a clean copy of the original, cleaned of unstable cases, and reviewed by humans before being frozen [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].
4. Two scores were computed [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9]. The Programmatic score is the share of tests passed; the tests read text, buttons and values through the accessibility interface (the system layer that screen readers use). The VLM score uses a vision-language model (an AI that reads images) as a judge, which checks screenshots against statements about the original. An app that does not build scores zero.
5. They then analysed agent behaviour and code size for four of the models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12].

### Data and setup
- 250 tasks, 50 per platform [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7].
- Median original size: 49.3k lines of code on Ubuntu, 13.5k on macOS, 6.7k on Windows, 15.0k on Android [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].
- 10 models. GPT models ran in the Codex tool and all others in Claude Code [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28].
- Network access was blocked by default, and reference and test files were protected [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
- Runs per task are not reported. [I] Our reviewers think it was probably one run, because one single-run comparison reproduces a main-table score exactly [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- 35,000 recreation runs were used as training data for the transfer experiment [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 5].

### Key findings
- [V] GPT-6 Astra leads with an average of 58.06 (Programmatic 58.19, VLM 57.92). Next are Claude Opus 5 (44.16) and GPT-5.6 Sol (42.06); Qwen3.7-Plus is lowest (9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [V] Full fidelity is rare. The best model passes at least 90% of tests on 17.6% of apps and all tests on 2.8%; every other model reaches at most 5.53% and 0.8% [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [V] Agents copy what an interface contains better than what it does. Structure tests had the highest pass rate in 15 of 16 native comparisons, and the weakest category trailed by 9.1 to 34.4 points [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
- [V] Rebuilds are smaller: 89.4% have less code than the original (median 16.9% of its size), and 92.3% use fewer files [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15].
- [V] More code did not mean better fidelity. Among the four analysed models, Claude Opus 5 wrote the most code, while the top model GPT-6 Astra wrote the least on four of five platforms [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15].

- [V] Agents rarely checked their final work: the full "edit, relaunch, inspect" loop appears in only 23.6% to 47.5% of runs [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12].
- [V] Copying from the original seems rare: median exact-line overlap is 0.014% to 0.088% [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 18].

- [A] A finite test suite "cannot establish equivalence across all states and interaction paths" [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- [A] Public originals may be in the models' training data [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- [A] The behaviour and code analyses are descriptive, so they do not show cause and effect [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 3].
- [A] Android isolation is weaker, and Web cannot hide the source [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 10].
- [I] No confidence intervals and probably one run per task, so small gaps between models may not be stable [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [I] All authors are from Alibaba, and Qwen models serve as judge and as training-data generator. No conflict-of-interest statement is given [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 5]. The Qwen judge model scored lowest, so no favourable self-scoring is visible [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- [I] Model and tool are mixed up: GPT ran in Codex, the rest in Claude Code [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28].
- [I] One Web site that replayed copied content escaped the cheating detector and kept a 54.82% Programmatic score [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 47].
- [I] Code size and file counts are not quality measures [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].

- G2: the VLM judge is never checked against human ratings, and self-preference is not tested [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
- G4: agents' weak self-checking [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12] raises the question of whether better feedback loops would help.
- G5: the authors suggest newly built originals to reduce training-data risk [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
- G6: [I] there is no human-developer or human-steered condition.
- G8: it is the only project paper with native Android rebuilds [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7], but apps needing login or remote services were excluded [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 8].

Do not copy its weak points: report several runs, validate any AI judge against humans, and keep model and tool separate.

### Connections to other papers

- Agrees with kim2026programdistill: agents rebuilding web apps from a live original recover only 49.15% of workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11], and their self-checks miss errors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
- Only partly agrees with chen2025iwr. Both find interaction harder than static structure [@chen2025iwr, p. 16]. But here the visual score is below the programmatic score for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11], so "looks right but behaves wrong" is not supported in general.
- Places Design2Code and Interaction2Code as earlier, narrower web benchmarks [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 21].

## IWR-Bench: Can LVLMs reconstruct interactive webpage from a user interaction video?
> **Takeaway:** When AI models watch a video of someone using a website and try to rebuild it, even the best model (GPT-5) scores only 36.35 out of 100, and no model gets more than 25 on working interactions [@chen2025iwr, p. 8]. Making things work is much harder than making them look right, although part of this gap comes from how the scores are built [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Yang Chen, Minghao Liu, Yufan Shen, Yunwen Li, Tianyuan Huang, Xinyu Fang, et al. (21 authors) |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed) |
| Identifier | DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2509.24709 (arXiv 2509.24709) |
| Paper type | Benchmark with a large model comparison |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirectly) |

### In plain words
Earlier tests asked AI to turn a single screenshot of a webpage into code. Real websites, however, react when you click, type or scroll. This paper asks whether AI models that understand images and video can rebuild a webpage, including its behaviour, just by watching a screen recording of a person using it [@chen2025iwr, p. 2]. This is a form of reverse engineering from observed behaviour, not from a written description. It matters for us because it shows how far current models are from copying what an app does, not only what it looks like.

### How they did it
1. Trained annotators recorded videos while using 100 real websites. A browser extension logged every action, such as clicks and typing [@chen2025iwr, p. 5].
2. They also collected the site's images and icons. The file names were replaced (for example asset_001.png) so the model had to match pictures by how they look [@chen2025iwr, p. 5].
3. Each model got the video (one frame per second, at most 64 frames) plus one image showing all assets. It had to write a single index.html file with all HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no outside libraries and any server behaviour faked in JavaScript [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
4. An "agent-as-a-judge" (an AI agent that operates the generated page) replayed the recorded actions on the new page [@chen2025iwr, p. 6]. Gemini-2.5-Pro judged whether each expected result happened [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
5. Two scores were combined [@chen2025iwr, p. 7]. IFS (Interactive Functionality Score) is the share of actions that work. VFS (Visual Fidelity Score) measures how similar the reached screens look. The Final Score is 0.7 x IFS + 0.3 x VFS.
6. The weights were tuned so the score matched human ratings as closely as possible [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].

### Data and setup
- 113 tasks from 100 websites, cut down from 200 candidates [@chen2025iwr, p. 5].
- 1,001 recorded actions (8.9 per video on average), with 620 visual checkpoints and 403 logic checks [@chen2025iwr, p. 6].
- Task mix: 7.96% static, 47.79% simple state, 33.63% complex workflow, 10.62% algorithm or game [@chen2025iwr, p. 3].
- 28 model entries: 17 commercial, 9 open-source and 2 video-specialised models. Three models were also run in a "thinking" mode [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
- Human checks: five PhD-level raters scored 60 outputs, and three PhD students watched the judge agent on 100 pages [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
- Runs per model and random seeds are not reported [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].

### Key findings
- [V] GPT-5 is best with Final 36.35, IFS 24.39 and VFS 64.25. No model exceeds 25 IFS [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
- [V] IFS is below VFS for every model, for example Claude-Sonnet-4 22.29 vs 61.34 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8]. [I] Part of this gap comes from the metric design: VFS only counts screens that were reached, while IFS counts every action [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
- [V] The top eight models are all commercial. The best open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking), scores 31.15 and beats 9 of the 17 commercial models. Video-specialised models are lowest (13.67 and 10.07) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
- [V] "Thinking" modes raise the Final Score only slightly (for example 34.62 vs 34.00) and lower VFS in all three pairs [@chen2025iwr, p. 8]. [A] The authors still call the gains "Consistent but Moderate" [@chen2025iwr, p. 9].
- [V] Scores drop sharply from static to interactive tasks: GPT-5 gets 61.85 on static pages but 25.26 on algorithm or game tasks [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
- [V] The judge agent failed in only 3 of 100 observed runs, and these errors were fixed [@chen2025iwr, p. 9].
- [V] Score weights matched human ratings only moderately: Spearman correlation 0.57 for VFS and 0.65 for the Final Score [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] The paper has no limitations section [@chen2025iwr, p. 9].
- [I] VFS and IFS use different denominators, so "visual is much better than function" is partly built in [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
- [I] Code quality is never measured. The single-file output is far from how real apps are built [@chen2025iwr, p. 20].
- [I] Gemini-2.5-Pro is both a judge and an evaluated model, and self-preference was not tested [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
- [I] The weights were tuned and tested on the same 60 human-rated items, with no held-out check [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
- [I] No repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests, so small differences such as 30.36 vs 30.31 may be noise [@chen2025iwr, p. 9].
- [I] Websites like IMDb may be in training data, and the authors do not discuss this [@chen2025iwr, p. 2].
- [I] The static and algorithm groups hold only about 9 and 12 tasks [@chen2025iwr, p. 3].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- G1: behaviour and looks are scored, code quality is not [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
- G2: the judge is calibrated in-sample and is also an evaluated model [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
- G5: [I] no contamination discussion was found.
- [A] The authors point to temporal reasoning, linking assets to the right places, and better state management as next steps [@chen2025iwr, p. 9].
- [I] The project's gap report dropped "visual beats functional" as a gap, because here it is partly a measurement artefact [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].

### Why it matters for your research
[I] IWR-Bench shows that rebuilding interactive behaviour from observation is hard for every model tested. Its action-replay judge and its split into "works" and "looks right" scores are useful ideas for your own study. Learn from its weaknesses too: give both scores the same denominator, use a judge that is not also tested, run each model more than once, and add code-quality measures. Treat its numbers as weak evidence, because this is a single preprint.

### Connections to other papers
- Builds on si2025benchmarking and xiao2025benchmarking. [A] The authors describe Design2Code as static and Interaction2Code as single-step and stateless [@chen2025iwr, p. 2].
- Agrees with xiao2025benchmarking: interactive parts score lower than full pages for all six models there [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
- Only directionally consistent with bai2026recreationworld. Static structure beats interaction there as well [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16], but its visual score is below its functional score for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
- Agrees with the agent studies that whole-app fidelity is low [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @yang2026programbench, p. 6].
- Scores cannot be ranked against other benchmarks, because each uses a different scoring method [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
